This refers to a case where one first employs a means while still a śrāmaṇera; before the act is completed, one receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*), and only after the ordination is concluded does the prior act finally come to fruition.
One may spontaneously incur the three *pārājika* offenses, because sexual misconduct cannot be preceded by the prior application of preparatory means.
Second, there is obstruction due to the deficiency of conditions; this refers to the failure to achieve the result because the necessary conditions are lacking.
Although conditions (*pratyaya*) are immeasurable, they can be subsumed without exceeding the three general and three specific types.
Regarding the three general conditions, they are as described in the *Vidyāmātra-śāstra* (*Prakaraṇapāda*).

Regarding the three specific conditions, those found in the Vinaya concerning the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*)—that is, the mind regarding the object—and the texts on the various offenses (*saṃvara-pāpaka*) are precisely these.
The detailed classification of karma consists of seven types, as has already been discussed above.
To briefly distinguish the cases of killing where the conditions are deficient, there are seven preparatory acts (*prayoga*):

first, the deficiency of the basis (*āśraya-prayoga*), which was formerly called the "deficiency of conditions" (*pratyaya-prayoga*); this was changed to "deficiency of the basis" because the former term was overly broad and confused with the general category.

This means that the Buddha's formulation of the precepts was based upon fully ordained bhikṣus; if one were to abandon the precepts only after having already conceived the intention to commit an offense, it would render the resulting transgression without a basis for formal adjudication.

Furthermore, the second case—when the detailed rules have not yet been established—and the third case—such as those afflicted by insanity or other maladies—are likewise not bases for the adjudication of a resultant transgression.
This establishes the present meaning by omitting the common condition; the following six types likewise omit the specific condition, which can be understood by investigating them.
Regarding the second [type], the object is powerful: one intends to kill another person, but because the person—the object—is powerful, they cannot be harmed.

The third is the error of intention (*abhiprāya-viparyaya*), such as using a knife or striking with a blow; the masters of old called this "discrepancy of conditions" (*pratyaya-viparyaya*), but it has been changed here because that term was also used too broadly as a general designation.
The fourth is the discrepancy of the object (*viṣaya-viparyaya*), which corresponds to the latter two phrases within the category of "perception regarding the object."

Although there are three categories of distinctions regarding the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*), none of them—being either "inferior" or "doubtful"—constitute a discrepancy in the object itself.

For instance, suppose one intends to kill a human being and advances toward him, but at the final moment, a non-human being comes to take his place; yet, one perceives the figure before one as the intended person and suspects it to be that very person. Since the actual object—the human being—is in fact absent, there is no offense resulting from the fruit of the act, though one does incur an offense regarding a different object.
Before being dispatched, one may encounter an obstacle on the way due to some offense; this is why it is called "obstructed by the boundary" (*jing-chai*).

When dispatched from a different territory, although there may be differences such as humans, animals, or insentient objects, none of them are the person originally intended; therefore, they are called "non-persons" (*fei-ren*).
There is no need for further elaboration.
The fifth transformation, perception (*saṃjñā*), and the sixth transformation, doubt (*vicikitsā*), correspond to the second and third phrases within the category of perception regarding the object.
This refers to cases where one originally intends toward a correct object, but at the moment of action, the perception undergoes a transformation.
The seventh is "cessation of mind," which refers to the mind that has ceased its urgent exertion but has not yet reached the fruit.
These seven stages of expedient means all lack the designation of "fruit" and are collectively termed "deficiency of conditions."
Within the karma of skillful means (*upāya-karman*), there are those that are distant and those that are proximate, or some that are entirely without fault.
For instance, regarding the abandonment of the precepts: if one first abandons the precepts and subsequently kills, there is no violation of the precepts at all.
Alternatively, if one has already formed the intention [to kill] and only then abandons the precepts, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
In some cases, the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is distant and constitutes a light *sthūlātyaya*; in others, the preparatory effort is proximate and constitutes a heavy *sthūlātyaya*.
Cases such as when the object is forceful, when one loses track of the intention, or when the mind ceases, are all to be explained according to this principle.
Therefore, the Vinaya text states: "If it is accomplished, it is a *pārājika*; if it is not accomplished, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This meaning contains distinctions.
When performing repentance, one must understand the gravity of the offense; this is not like the ancients who merely counted the names and categories without comprehending these distinctions.
This concludes the brief exposition on the meaning of skillful means.

Regarding the ancient masters' further explanations on the categories of upholding and violating the precepts, I have now examined them in detail; since each instance of violation corresponds precisely to its respective textual passage, there is no need for a separate summary.

As for that which maintains [the precepts], it consists of the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right situational awareness (*samyak-samprajanya*); guarding the six sense faculties so that they do not leak out and cause the afflictions of breaking the precepts is what is called "maintaining."

There are two types of observance: that which consists of ceasing evil and that which consists of cultivating the wholesome; these are what the ancients called *virati-dhāraṇī* (observance of cessation) and *karaṇa-dhāraṇī* (observance of action).
Furthermore, there are precepts that possess both cessation and action, as well as those that are exclusively either cessation or action alone; one should reflect upon this to attain realization.
However, there are two kinds of evil:
first, action (vastu), and second, phenomena (dharma).
Action refers to such things as sexual misconduct, while phenomena refer to such things as falsehood; both of these two types must be brought to cessation.
Wholesomeness (*kuśala*) also has two aspects:
first, action (*vastu*), and second, phenomena (*dharma*).
Action refers to that which should be performed, such as constructing a dwelling in accordance with the teachings, as explained in the *Śilapatala* and other treatises.
"Dharma" refers to that which should be studied, such as the recitation of the precepts and so forth.
One should apply oneself to the study of both these types; to cease the mind's effort and fail to study is indolence.
Furthermore, not understanding them constitutes lack of correct knowledge (*asamprajanya*), or it may be ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because these afflictions cause the body and speech to undergo transformation, they constitute the two offenses of non-learning and ignorance.
The Vinaya also clearly states that one must have completed five years of seniority to be authorized to recite the Prātimokṣa and perform the *karmavācanā*.

It is further stated: "If one does not know and does not see the five groups of offenses, I say that such a person is deluded, having committed a *pārājika* offense, even down to being one of evil speech.
These words are concise yet rich in meaning, with no principle left unaddressed; how could they compare to the ancient masters who used prolixity and redundant phrasing?
The text for "Carefully Maintaining" should be understood as previously explained.
Next, the second section is interpreted, divided into three parts:
first, clarifying the teachings upon which it relies; second, enumerating the names and characteristics of the offenses; and third, concluding with the instruction to carefully maintain them.
Therefore, regarding the transgression of the precepts through leakage, there are generally six types of objects of violation mentioned in the Vinaya:
first, internal form, which refers to the form of sentient beings;
second, external form, which refers to insentient things.
Third, internal and external forms, which refers to the combination of these two types of form.
Fourth, water, which refers to moving the body against or with the current of water.
Fifth, wind, and sixth, space; these should be understood by analogy with water.
Except for those occurring in dreams, one does not incur the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
However, there are five faults associated with sleeping with a distracted mind according to the Vinaya:

first, having bad dreams; second, not being protected by the devas; third, the mind not entering into the Dharma; fourth, failing to contemplate the signs of light; and fifth, emitting semen during sleep.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, sleeping with a distracted mind constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā* states: "If a bhikṣu sleeps while maintaining a mental image—having first prepared the means by interlacing his feet and clasping his hands while forming such an image—and semen is emitted during sleep, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
Regarding the opening of the precept text, it is because the previous [precepts] lacked the preliminary expedient means.
Second, the precept on physical contact.

According to the Vinaya, if both parties are without clothing, physical contact incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if either one has clothing, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if both have clothing, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Hair and nails are still parts of one's own body, and are therefore considered "remnants" (*śeṣa*).
According to the *Sammohavinodanī*, if hair touches hair or a nail touches a nail, one incurs only a *thullaccaya* offense because neither possesses sensation;
however, if they mutually possess sensation, it constitutes a *saṃghādisesa*, as stated in the text of the precepts.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi), fascicle five, states: "Regarding 'women,' this refers to one's mother, daughters, sisters, relatives or non-relatives, whether elder or younger, whether lay or ordained; [to engage with any of them] constitutes an offense."
According to the Vinaya, if a dead woman’s body is largely intact, touching her also constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Third is the precept against coarse speech:
to speak words of sexual desire to a woman with a defiled mind for one's own gratification constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma with a pure mind, rebukes the faults of desire, and so forth, there is no offense.
Regarding "a woman," she must be intelligent and not yet deceased; this differs from the preceding precept.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if a woman addresses a bhikṣu with coarse language with a defiled mind, the monk who accepts it also commits an offense.
Fourth is the precept against praising one's own body and soliciting offerings.
To feign the Buddha-dharma as a pretext for inducing others to recite [the scriptures] does not constitute a grave offense; therefore, it is only a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Fifth is the precept against matchmaking:
because it unites the cycle of birth and death, it constitutes a profound loss of right mindfulness.
To speak with, write letters to, or dispatch messengers for them all constitutes a transgression of the limits.
Whenever one receives a letter to be delivered, it must be examined before being carried; failure to examine it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, as explained in the Vinaya.
Sixth, the precept against constructing a dwelling by requesting more materials than necessary.
This precept comprises two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses, totaling four transgressions.

In the enumeration of their names, only the name *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is explicitly revealed; this is because the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses constitute the primary category of this section, and thus the names of the *duṣkṛta* offenses are omitted.
The text consists of three sections:
first, the person who commits the offense; second, the explanation of compliance and violation; and third, the conclusion regarding the offense of violation.
Within the second section, compliance is explained first, followed by the analysis of violation.
What is called "in accordance" refers to performing the ritual in conformity with the teachings.
First, "seeking for oneself" means begging from a donor.
Second, "building a house. Third, "without an owner" serves to distinguish and exclude [other cases].
This means that although one may beg for oneself, it is sometimes possible to obtain a donor through begging;

however, the intent here is to distinguish cases where there is ultimately no donor at all. Thus the Vinaya states: "Regarding 'one without an owner,' there is no person [acting as a donor], whether one, two, or many."
4. "For oneself" excludes the non-offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* when acting for another.
5. "It should be made according to measure": according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, this is one span of the Buddha’s hand, which is two chi (尺).
Excluding the interior of the room, it should measure four *zhang*, which is twenty-four feet.
Sixth, “One should point out the location to the bhikṣu” means instructing him on how to request the ritual procedure.

This means that the owner of the dwelling first prepares the site by clearing it of obstacles and difficulties, then enters the Saṃgha and makes three formal requests to the community. The Saṃgha then dispatches a messenger.
The owner of the dwelling takes the messenger to inspect the location and confirms that it is free of obstacles and difficulties.
"Obstruction" refers to hindrances to monastic affairs, even to the extent that a grass cart cannot turn around there.
"Danger" refers to places where there are many tigers, wolves, and lions, down to even ants.

7. Regarding the phrase, "That bhikṣu shall point out a location that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions," it means that the Saṃgha has formally granted permission through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to carry out the construction at that site.
"If a bhikṣu builds [a dwelling] in a place where there is danger, or even if he builds it in excess of the prescribed measure," this explains the transgression of the teaching.
Many monasteries in mountain regions violate this precept.
Even Arhats have fallen away due to the causes of extensive worldly affairs; how much more so should one who dwells among the ignorant and foolish not be heedful?
Since physical well-being allows the Path to flourish, he further opens the allowance for one to act according to what is appropriate.
Many people occupy themselves with their own appearance, obstructing the affairs of the Sangha; such a dwelling is unsuitable and leads to self-destruction.
Out of compassion, the Sangha deliberated and granted them the Dharma; this is the reason for the establishment of these regulations.
Seventh is the precept against building a house without authorization from the owner.
This precept entails one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) offense and two *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offenses; it is designated as "only manifesting the formal meeting" offense.
The text also consists of three sections, with the second section distinguishing five phrases regarding compliance.
First, "intending to build a large dwelling": since there is a donor, even if it is built on a large scale, the undertaking is not abandoned.

Second, "having an owner"; third, "building for oneself"; fourth, "the method of requesting [materials]"; fifth, "the formal act of giving. Next, the violations of these rules shall be distinguished, as can be understood.
Question:
Since the two remaining cases in the preceding section have already been combined into a single rule, why not include this remaining case as well to make three? Answer:

The phrasing is straightforward and the meanings are mutually dependent; therefore, the two remaining cases regarding the "excessive" and "immeasurable" [robes] were combined into one rule for the preceding category.
Since the meanings are already contradictory and the phrasing would become cumbersome, they are formulated as separate rules.
Eighth, the precept against falsely accusing a bhikṣu of a grave offense without basis.
This text consists of eight phrases.
First, the person who may commit the offense.
2. Regarding "because of being obscured by hatred," one falsely gives rise to malice toward those who have committed no transgression.
3. Regarding "a bhikṣu who is not one guilty of a pārājika offense," this refers to the object of the slander.

Because this text is concise, it merely clarifies that one does not commit a *pārājika* offense; however, according to the Vinaya, even if one has actually committed such an act, as long as the person being slandered lacks the three criteria (*trīṇi mūlāni*), it is likewise termed "not a *pārājika*."

Therefore, the Vinaya text states: "If that person is not pure, and one has not seen, heard, or suspected that they have committed a *pārājika* offense, yet one says, 'I have seen, heard, or suspected that they have committed a *pārājika* offense.'"
"To defame another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
There are six detailed cases, as explained in the Vinaya, which cannot be recounted here at length.

Furthermore, if the person being accused is not one of the thirteen types of persons ineligible for ordination (*anantarāyika*), yet one falsely accuses them of being so, this also constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The eight *pārājika* offenses for slandering a nun, as well as the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, are likewise all violations of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
these are all as explained in the Vinaya. Fourth, regarding "without basis": there are briefly three bases upon which an accusation may rest, namely, what has been seen, heard, or suspected;
since there is now no such basis, it is called "without basis."
If one personally witnesses the commission of sexual misconduct, theft, or similar acts, it is called the "root of seeing.
If another person sees such acts and comes to report them to me, this is also the root of seeing.
If one personally hears of the commission of sexual misconduct, theft, or similar matters, as well as when others hear of them, these are both termed the "root of hearing."
There are two roots of doubt:

first, the arising of doubt from personally witnessing traces of activity, such as seeing a bhikṣu entering or leaving a forest with a woman and thereby suspecting him of committing sexual misconduct; cases of theft and so forth should be understood by analogy.
Second, the arising of doubt upon hearing sounds directly; that is, hearing such sounds as those of moving a bed with a woman, or likewise those of a thief and so forth.
These two types together are termed the "root of doubt."
When another person comes to me with doubts, these too constitute the root of doubt.

These three roots—seeing, hearing, and doubting—are precisely what are fit for bringing forth an accusation. Apart from these three roots, if one suddenly and arbitrarily gives rise within the mind to perceptions of seeing, hearing, or doubting, or to three types of arbitrary doubts, and speaks according to one's own inclinations, although there is no offense of slander, it does not constitute a formal accusation; this is because the person has no fault and lacks witnesses to corroborate it.
5. Regarding "defaming with a *pārājika* offense," this distinguishes it from other minor defamations which do not constitute an infraction of this precept.
6. Regarding "desiring to destroy their pure conduct," this clarifies the mental state that initiates the karmic action.
7. From "If at another time" onwards, it refers to confessing one's own guilt.
The matter of Dharmatāpa’s purity can be verified; he either confessed under interrogation or confessed without being interrogated.
He bowed his head and said:
"I know that this matter was indeed groundless, but I spoke these words out of anger.
8. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the offense is defined as in the text.
Ninth, the precept against falsely accusing a bhikṣu on the basis of a grave offense.
The text consists of nine clauses.
First, the person who may commit the offense.

2. "Because of anger. 3. Regarding "taking a portion from a different category," the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (The Good Vision), chapter thirteen, states: "'Another part' refers to the following: Tvaṣṭṛ is a human being, while a sheep is a non-human being; to substitute the sheep for the position of Tvaṣṭṛ is called 'another part.'"
To treat a ewe as a *bhikṣuṇī* is also called "the remaining portion. Why?
Because the circumstances are similar.
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states that one takes a "portion.
The *Shu* (Commentary) says: "Taking a portion from within a different category means calculating based on similarity.
As it is said in the Vinaya:
The bhikṣu Maitrībala descended from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and saw a large ram engaging in sexual intercourse with a ewe.
He immediately said to his companion: "This ram is none other than Upavāna, and the ewe is the bhikṣuṇī Maitrī."
He then addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"I saw with my own eyes that Upāli (Tapassu) committed sexual misconduct with the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyanī.

Although the bhikṣu Maitrāyanī had intentionally given the ram the name Upāli when he spoke to the Saṃgha—and thus his statement was not baseless—he did so only in the hope that the Saṃgha would believe him and unjustly punish Upāli; therefore, this is called a "false ground" (*mūlaka*).

In the case of "seeing roots upon a sheep," although it appears to be a formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), the accusation is actually groundless (*amūlaka*) regarding Dharmapāla; therefore, it constitutes slander.
This is omitted from the text of the precepts.

According to the Vinaya, "false grounds" (*mṛṣāmūla*) include: falsely attributing an offense of the lower category, falsely attributing it to another person, falsely attributing it to a time when one was a layperson, and falsely attributing it to the echo of one's own voice. All such cases are termed "false grounds."
If one actually sees an offense but says they have heard of it, then since the claim of having heard it is non-existent, this constitutes a groundless charge (*amūlaka*), not a pretextual ground.
Fourth, regarding "a bhikṣu who is not subject to pārājika," those who are actually not among the thirteen grounds for defeat (*anantarāya*) are nonetheless included within this category.
5. “Because of the lack of basis”: although the sheep has a root [organ], Upāli lacks one.
6. “Defaming with a *pārājika* offense”; 7. the arising of the karmic mind; 8. self-accusation; 9. the formal determination of the offense.
Tenth: The precept against causing a schism in the Saṃgha despite being exhorted to desist.

Regarding a general analysis: all forms of exhortation involve potential confusion; in principle, one must distinguish between types of exhortation, which should be understood according to their respective meanings.
However, there are two types of defiance of admonition:

first, defiance of the Sangha’s admonition, such as these four admonitions, as well as the three Sangha admonitions mentioned below regarding the refusal to acknowledge that one's desire does not constitute an obstacle;
second, defiance of private admonition, such as the *pāyattika* offense for one who refuses admonition within the ninety [rules].
Question:
Since both equally disregard the Sangha’s admonition, why is there a difference between the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and the *pāyattika* offenses? Answer:
There are many reasons for the varying degrees of gravity regarding the commission of offenses.

For instance, the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha through agitation is particularly grave; therefore, when plotting together, one should first advise the leader, because if the leader desists, the others will also desist.
Since the leader does not desist, his assistance in fanning the fire with fuel makes the transgression even more severe; therefore, he must again be admonished.

As for those who defile the community and incite slander—accumulating faults within the village for a long time such that they cause others to lose their pure faith—and those who, having been expelled, ought to submit but instead slander the Saṃgha in return: their transgressions are likewise not light, and thus they too should be admonished.

One who is of a malicious nature, who rejects the Saṃgha, exalts himself, and treats the assembly with contempt, is difficult to tolerate; therefore, he must be admonished. Should he persist in defiance, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

As stated in the *Lalita-vistara*, one who claims that desire does not constitute an obstacle and holds such perverse views as being correct—even if the Saṃgha offers admonition—will not have his mental attachments opened. If one were to impose a heavy offense (*pārājika*) upon him, it would be inappropriate; therefore, he only incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
However, an ancient difficulty is raised:

if it is the case that the gravity of the offense of *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (the sin of opposing admonition) increases according to the accumulation of faults such as defiling the household, then since the matter of private admonition (*raho-vāda*) pertains to all seven classes of offenses (*sapta-nikāya*), why not apply this principle directly to the specific cases to determine the varying degrees of gravity for the offense of opposing admonition?

Now, regarding "defiling the household," this refers to long-term transgressions arising within a village that have accumulated into many offenses. Although the private admonition mentions all seven categories of offenses (*saptāpatti-nikāya*), it may be that the person in question intended only to commit one and did not intend to commit many; how, then, can this be equated with the many transgressions of defiling a household?
The Bhikṣuṇīs have separate precepts, which should likewise be applied according to the general principles; they cannot be recounted here in detail.
The text of the precepts consists of three parts:
first, those who may commit the offense; second, the method of admonition; and third, the establishment of the offense for refusing admonition.
The second method of admonition consists of two pairs of four phrases:
regarding the first pair, if a transgression arises, one should first offer private admonition;
regarding the second pair, if one disregards private admonition, it is proper that the Saṃgha offer admonition.
The meaning of all admonitions regarding the precepts is identical to this.
Within the context of the arising of transgressions, there are four points of meaning:
first, "one who wishes to destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha" refers to the initial arousal of the karmic mind.
Regarding the phrase "the method of using skillful means to bring about the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha," there are two types:

first, the use of skillful means to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, such as in the case of Devadatta, who himself acted as a false Buddha and caused four evil companions to constitute a false Saṃgha; because he devised a scheme to break the Saṃgha, it is called "skillful means."
Second is the practice of destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha by collectively accepting and practicing five kinds of heterodox dharmas as the "jewel of heterodox dharma.

Regarding these five heterodoxies: first, begging for food for the duration of one's life; second, wearing rag-robes; third, sitting in the open air; fourth, not consuming ghee or salt; and fifth, not eating fish or meat.

Regarding the fourth meaning, "firmly maintaining without abandoning": it refers to falsely relying upon and taking refuge in a counterfeit Triple Gem, stubbornly upholding it to compete with the Buddha in propagation and thereby destroying the True Wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the private admonition, according to the Vinaya, it applies to the admonition of all seven classes of practitioners as well as non-Buddhists; for now, we shall discuss the admonition of bhikṣus.
The text consists of two sections:
first, the exhortation to cease the four transgressions, as found in the text.
2. From "Venerable sir, you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha" onwards, [the text] refutes that person's persistent attachment.
To refute by saying "you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha" is to refute the initial arising of the mind that initiates the action.
"To be in harmony and joy with the Saṃgha" refutes the plotting of schemes.
"Not disputing" refutes the establishment of the five heterodox dharmas.

From "studying under the same teacher" onwards, it exhorts one to reverse competitive transformations, so that one may attain the increase of the path toward enlightenment and realize the peace and bliss of the realized path.
Next, the second [stage] is explained.
If one violates the private admonition, it is logically necessary that the Saṃgha admonish him.
Regarding the phrase, "When this bhikṣu is thus being admonished, he stubbornly maintains his position and does not relinquish it," this refers to violating the private admonition.
Regarding the passage beginning with "That bhikṣu should be admonished three times," there are two parts within it:
first, instructing the Saṃgha to admonish him to relinquish [the position]; second, praising relinquishment as virtuous.
This means that praising the act of relinquishing—which is the opposite of contrariness—actually constitutes a virtuous compliance.

Regarding "the three admonitions": one formal announcement (*jñapti*) expresses the propriety of the matter, followed by three *karmavācanā* (formal acts of the Saṃgha). At the third moment [of the third *karmavācanā*], one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Prior to the third [moment], it is still possible to desist; therefore, it is described as "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
The claim that the ancients took one motion (*ñatti*) and two proclamations (*kammavācā*) as constituting the three admonitions is incorrect.
"If he does not relinquish it at the third [admonition], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*" is precisely the formal definition of the offense for defying the admonition.

Since ancient times, various masters have largely relied upon the śāstras to analyze and refute the breaking of the Wheel of Dharma; yet after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, such an event certainly did not occur, as it would be logically impossible to commit such a transgression.

Now, examining the intent of the Vinaya, it differs slightly from the śāstras: while the śāstras analyze the immediate karmas (ānantarya-karma), they restrict the definition of this specific karma to Devadatta alone.

The intent of the present Vinaya text is as follows: even if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, someone establishes a separate heterodox teaching and uses voting sticks (*śalākā*) to convert people to their own views—though this is not strictly categorized as an immediate offense (*ānantarya-karma*)—it nonetheless causes affliction to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha must therefore offer a formal admonition; if the person does not relinquish their position despite the admonition, they incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Therefore, the Vinaya text states: "There are two matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha: first, performing a *karmavācanā*; second, taking up the voting sticks (*śalākā*).

According to the Śāstra, taking up the voting sticks constitutes an immediate offense (*ānantarya-karma*); according to the Vinaya, this is explained comprehensively, hence it says "performing the *karmavācanā*."
Although the categories of meaning for these precepts are extensive and manifold, their practical application is concise; therefore, they are explained briefly as such.
Eleventh: The offense of assisting in a schism of the Sangha in violation of admonitions.
The text also has three parts:
first, the person who may commit the offense; second, the method of admonition; and third, the establishment of the offense for refusing admonition.
Regarding the second part, the method of admonition, there are two pairs of fourfold propositions:
First, if a transgression arises, one should first offer private admonition; second, if they persist in defiance of that private admonition, it is proper for the Saṃgha to offer formal admonition.
Within the section on the arising of transgressions, there are two phrases:
"whether one, or two, or even an infinite number," which refers to committing transgressions while acting as a companion or associate.
There are two types of accomplices:
first, the primary accomplice, who originally conspired together with the intent that four or more persons constitute a group of heterodox monks;
second, the assisting accomplice, who later aids in the evil deed, whether there be one, two, or even an infinite number, being unrestricted by quantity.
If both of these companions should assist in committing an evil act, they are both termed "companions," and both must be admonished.
Second, that bhikṣu says to this bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!..."
"Do not admonish this bhikṣu," and so forth; this refers to speaking out to provide assistance.
As it says in the Vinaya, when the various bhikṣus were admonishing Devadatta, some of his companions said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not admonish Devadatta."

Devadatta is a monk who speaks according to the Dharma and is worthy of emulation; he is a monk who speaks according to the Vinaya and is skilled in training and transforming others. What Devadatta has spoken, we rejoice in and find rare to hear; we receive it upon our heads, and with deep hearts, we accept, approve, and accord with it.
Since there is the aforementioned fault, the following text correctly analyzes the private admonition (*raho-’nuśāsanā*), which also consists of two sections:
first, the admonition to cease mutual assistance, as in the text;
second, from “However, the bhikṣu speaks what is not the Dharma” onwards, it removes their persistent attachment.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Twelfth is the precept concerning slandering the Saṃgha and defying admonition when undergoing banishment.
This section also has three parts:
First, the person who commits the offense; second, the method of admonition; third, the formal definition of the offense for refusing admonition.
Regarding the second, the method of admonition, there are two pairs of fourfold propositions, as previously determined.
Within the section on transgressions, there are two statements:
first, being expelled by the Saṃgha due to defiling the household; second, slandering the Saṃgha unreasonably while under expulsion.
This unreasonable slander of the Saṃgha is precisely the matter for which he is to be admonished.
Within the preceding section on the *bhaṇḍana* (reception), the text further contains two sub-sections.
The first concerns the defilement of families and misconduct within towns and villages.
Regarding the term "defiling a family" (*kuladūṣaka*), according to the Vinaya, there are four types:
First, regarding defiling one's family:

for example, if one receives a gift from the Zhang family and sends it to the Wang family, the Zhang family will hear of it and lose faith, becoming displeased; meanwhile, the Wang family, having received the object, will think only of repaying that specific kindness, thereby losing their impartial faith.
Second, defiling a family by means of gain:
although one has acquired wealth in accordance with the Dharma, one gives it to one householder and not to another householder.
Third, defiling a family by means of intimate friends.
This refers to acting with partiality toward kings and ministers—favoring one person while excluding another.
Fourth is defiling the household by relying on a monastery (*saṃghārāma*).

This means taking the flowers or fruits belonging to the Saṃgha and giving them to one person while withholding them from another; because this causes the former person to lose their sense of equanimity, it is called "defiling the household."

"Evil conduct" refers to such acts as planting flowers oneself or instructing others to plant them, or eating from the same bed or using the same utensils as a woman, and so forth—including all manner of improper behaviors ranging from the most serious offenses (saṃghāvaśeṣa) down to minor transgressions (pāyattika).
Having committed these two acts of defiling the household through evil conduct, they were seen and heard by both the monastics and the laity.

Second, regarding the passage from "The bhikṣus should speak to the bhikṣu" down to "he need not remain here," this follows the *vinaya* texts in performing the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to expel him and remove him from the village where he has been practicing.

Now, regarding what appears in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* to be the words of another person stating that one is to be expelled: this is because such verbal expression already exists within the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).
Second, concerning the irrational slander of the Saṃgha, the meaning of the text states: "The bhikṣu who has been banished says to the other bhikṣus:
'You possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; for what reason do you still grant me [rehabilitation]? "
"Why do the bhikṣus who committed the same offense as I not drive them into exile, yet exile me alone?

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, at that time six people had collectively defiled the household; hearing that the Saṃgha intended to exile them, Srenika and Māhīsaka fled to the village of Rājagṛha, while Kālodāyin and Chanda met them on the road to offer their repentance.
These four persons fled and could not be treated; they offered no repentance and were thus without absolution.
Only Āśvalāyana and Pūrṇaśas fled neither nor repented, and consequently were expelled by the Saṃgha.
Thereupon, they slandered the Sangha, saying:
"Those who love others' confessions and those who fear others and flee were not driven away;
it is because we two have provoked their anger that we alone have been driven out."
"Since there are already these three—attachment, aversion, and fear—it is known that they are fully possessed of the affliction of delusion.
This concludes the passage concerning the arising of faults.
Next, the explanation of private admonition, cessation, and deprivation follows; this should be understood according to the preceding [rules].

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun), fascicle four, states: "If a bhikṣu seeks anything whatsoever—whether for the sake of the Triple Gem or for himself—and gives various articles of faith to kings, ministers, elders, lay householders, or those who have left the home life, it is all termed 'defiling the family' (*kuladūṣaka*)."
The five assemblies are not permitted [to do so] at all; even weeping for the death of parents is entirely forbidden.
For the four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅), while for a nun, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (逸提).
The detailed exposition of what is permitted and what is prohibited is fully contained in that treatise.

The thirteenth precept concerns using one's own will to reject exhortation and disobey admonition; its older name was the precept against being of evil character and rejecting the Sangha’s admonition.
This text also has three parts:
first, the person who commits the offense; second, the method of admonition; and third, the formal definition of the offense of disobeying admonition.
Regarding the second method of admonition, within the two pairs of four statements, there are first two points concerning the one who initiates the transgression:
first, "being of an evil nature and refusing to accept the words of others" distinguishes the fault of acting according to one's own will while rejecting exhortation.
The secular classics state, "He who asks much becomes ample; he who uses his own will alone becomes small," which is precisely this point.
Second, from the phrase "Within the precepts and laws" onwards, there is a discernment of the characteristics of one who uses their own will and does not accept admonition.

That is to say, when one has violated the precepts, others advise one to desist; yet one receives the offerings of the faithful in vain, being arrogant and self-opinionated by nature, and says to others:
"Do not speak to me of what is good or evil, nor of the good results of good conduct or the evil results of evil conduct."
This fool’s intention was: “I understand for myself the fruits of karma and their retribution; when the retribution is experienced, it is none of your business.

As for my saying ‘I will not speak to you of whether it is good or evil,’ you yourself have already spoken regarding the fruits of your own karma. Thus he concluded: “Cease now and do not admonish me.”
Traditionally, it has been handed down that there are four types of persons who must be admonished:

first, those of venerable seniority and virtue; second, those who have long occupied the leadership of the community; third, those who are extensively learned and deliberative, meaning their wisdom surpasses others; and fourth, those who dwell together with superior persons.
Next, the private admonition is explained; this refers to the refusal to accept counsel prior to the admonition, as she persisted in her own way.
The text also consists of two sections:
the first is the exhortation to cease her self-willed behavior.
Therefore, the text says: "That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable sir, do not yourself refuse to accept admonition.'"
The second [point] removes their stubborn attachment;
the text says, "Venerable sir, you yourself shall receive the words of admonition," and so forth.

Regarding "attaining increase" and so on: it means causing unarisen wholesome states to arise, preventing unarisen unwholesome states from arising, increasing wholesome states already arisen, and eliminating unwholesome states already arisen—these are to be applied respectively.
The remaining text follows the previous pattern.
From here on, the third section concludes the formal recitation:
"Venerable sirs, I have finished reciting the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. This marks the conclusion of the recitation.

*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (僧伽婆尸沙) is translated in the *Yogācāra* tradition as "remnant of the community" (*zhòngyú*). The old name is *sēngcán* (僧殘), where "remnant" (*cán*) carries the meaning of "residue" (*yú*).

This means that one who commits this offense cannot count toward the required quorum for nine types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*); however, in relation to other formal acts, it still possesses the residual utility of fulfilling the quorum.

Regarding the "nine karmas," these refer to: first, the four types of karma such as concealment; second, censure; third, banishment; fourth, dependence; fifth, prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople; and sixth, the place of offense.

Regarding the first four dharmas, they are fully elucidated in the *Pārājika-vastu* (the *Pārivāsika-khandhaka*), where their mutual deficiencies are detailed; as for the latter five types, their meaning has been established by tradition since antiquity.
Since both sets involve the forfeiture of thirty-five matters, they are like the seven groups of five found in the *Tarjanīya-khandhaka*.

Furthermore, regarding the first five [restrictions]: first, one may not bestow the full precepts upon others; second, one may not receive formal dependence (*niśraya*); third, one may not accept a novice (*śrāmaṇera*); fourth, one may not be appointed to instruct nuns; fifth, even if appointed, one may not go.
Such details are explained at length in the Vinaya; it is clear that when these individuals are considered in relation to one another, they do not count toward the required quorum.

Although those who have not seen their offense, have not confessed it, or have not abandoned their evil and heterodox views—those subject to the three types of formal suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*)—are likewise deprived of the thirty-five privileges, they cannot fulfill the total number of the entire Saṃgha when participating in a formal act of the assembly; therefore, they are not the same as those who are suspended for other reasons.

These residual offenses must rely upon the Saṃgha to be expiated; therefore, they are called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or "remaining with the community. There are further alternative explanations in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which cannot be recounted here at length.

From "The First Offense of the Nine Precepts" onwards, the method of repentance is briefly explained as a corollary; this section consists of six parts: first, distinguishing the conditions that constitute an offense;

second, clarifying the fault of concealment; third, revealing the method of repentance; fourth, explaining the deficiency of having fewer than the required number of monks; fifth, demonstrating that the community of monks bears culpability; and sixth, concluding with the proper application of the Dharma.

First, regarding the explanation of how an offense is established through the fulfillment of conditions, the text states: "In the first nine precepts, the offense is incurred upon the initial transgression; in the [final] four, it is incurred after three admonitions. This means that for the first nine precepts, the offense is established immediately upon the completion of the specific conditions regarding the matter;
for the latter four precepts, the offense is established once the three admonitions are completed, based on the fulfillment of conditions regarding the formal rule.
The intent here is to clarify that if the necessary conditions are not met, it does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, and thus the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* method of repentance cannot be applied;
this is why it is explained.

Some commentators interpret this as resolving a doubt: namely, since the latter four precepts are offenses committed before the assembly, one might think there is no need to treat the concealment (*praticchādana*). Therefore, the doubt is resolved by stating that the concealment must also be treated.

Now, upon careful examination, if that were the case, then regarding the previous nine offenses of concealment arising from doubt, there would be no instances where one does not conceal them; one should also resolve such doubts by stating that even if one does not conceal them, one is exempt from the punishment for concealment.
Since the text does not clarify this, it is evident that the [previous] interpretation was erroneous.
The second passage states: "If a bhikṣu commits any one of these offenses and knowingly conceals it," which clarifies that the offense of concealment is established.

According to the *Pudgala-vastu* (人犍度) and other Vinaya treatises, if one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and, with one's own mind, recognizes and perceives it as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (吉) for concealment by concealing it for even one night.
In this manner, as they pass from one to another, each night they incur the offense of *pācittiya* and the offense of *duṣkṛta* for concealment.
Even if, regarding the remaining offenses, there is doubt or ignorance, although they have committed the offense of concealment, they incur only the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one has committed concealment for two, three, or more instances, even to the point of not remembering the number, it is permitted to perform repentance.

However, according to the *Khandhaka* text of the Dharmaguptaka school, one first repents for the offense of concealment (*pācittiya*), and only afterwards does one request from the Saṃgha the disciplinary treatment for the concealed offense and carry out the practice of concealment (*parivāsa*).
Question:
Once the concealment has been confessed and the offense has been expiated, why is it necessary to request disciplinary treatment? Answer:

Although the retribution for a concealed offense has already vanished once the confession is made, it causes one to defile the pure Sangha, thereby making the residual offense more grave. Since this fault would not be punished and the residual offense would not be removed otherwise, it is necessary to penalize the concealment.
If one does not conceal [the offense], it causes the remaining transgression to be light; therefore, no punishment is administered for concealment.
Question:
Within the single category of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, how can there be degrees of lightness and heaviness?
Answer: Although they belong to the same category, this does not preclude differences in gravity.
For example, if an offender commits a transgression that is heavy in all three periods, how could this be the same as one who is light in two periods and heavy in one?
The third section, beginning with "One should forcibly grant," correctly reveals the method for repentance (*pratideśanā*).
As for the methods, there are either three or four; as for the stages, they are divided into five, or six, seven, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the five [types of parivāsa], the first is described in the text as "one should forcibly grant the *pārivāsika*"; according to the *Viniścaya-śāstra*, this is translated as *pūrvavāsa* (past dwelling); according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is translated as *pṛthagvāsa* (separate dwelling); and according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is translated as *pracchādana* (concealment).
"Concealment" (*paticchādana*) is a term applied by way of contrast to the offense.
"Parivāsa" (probation) is a disciplinary measure requiring one to stay alone in a quiet place to reflect upon one's transgression;
thus, the Vinaya text states: "One must not stay overnight in the same room with two or three others."
Regarding "having spent the night" (*rātri-vāsa*), it refers to having passed the night while practicing [the concealment].

When one is about to request this *paryuṣita-āpatti-vidhi* (the procedure for concealed offenses), one must clearly ascertain whether the number of offenses is one, two, many, or if the number is not remembered; furthermore, one must know whether the concealment lasted for one, two, many nights, or if the number of nights is not remembered. According to these facts, they should be recorded and included within the words of the formal request.
If one remembers the number of nights, one should beg according to that number of nights and proceed accordingly after begging.
If one does not remember the number of nights, one should beg from the time of purification and treat it accordingly; that is, from the day one received the precepts as the point of purification.
There are three ways of requesting the formal procedure (*jñapti*):

first, requesting with knowledge of the number of days; second, requesting without knowledge of the number of days; and third, requesting with partial knowledge and partial ignorance of the number of days—this refers to cases where one has committed many offenses, knowing the duration of some while being ignorant of others, and the number of offenses is likewise declared according to what is remembered.
The threefold request for the formula is explained in detail in the Vinaya.

Once the request has been made, the Saṃgha performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to grant the *parivāsa* (probation), all as prescribed in the Vinaya.
Regarding the phrase "grants [it] by force," the question is:
In the *Poṣadha-vastu*, there is a passage stating: "One must not coerce someone into confessing. Why is this called coercion? Answer:

In that case, if one coerces them at an inappropriate time, it leads to dispute; here, however, because the timing is appropriate and the Saṃgha is harmonious and accompanied by virtuous associates, one may therefore exercise coercion to raise the matter for disciplinary treatment.

Second, "the completion of the *parivāsa*": this means that if one commits a single *pārājika*-like offense and conceals it for one hundred days, one must undergo the *parivāsa* within the boundary (*sīmā*) for exactly those one hundred days before it can be said to be completed.
If there is at least one person within the boundary, one may immediately perform the practice.

While performing it, one must relinquish thirty-five matters and make offerings to the pure Saṃgha; furthermore, one must inform visiting bhikṣus so that they may know of the concealment and other such matters.
When eight conditions are fully met— as detailed in the *Prātimokṣa-vibhaṅga* section on concealment (*paryuṣitaka*)—
one may receive the "superior six-night *mānatva*," which is here translated as "pleasing the assembly."
This dharma must be performed within the boundary by at least four persons; it is called "pleasing the assembly.
This differs from the concealment [of offenses], where a single person may perform it, which is not called "pleasing the assembly."
Regarding "granting by way of increase" (*adhika-dāna*), there are two aspects to this granting:
first, one completes the *parivāsa* (probation); second, one requests it from the Saṃgha.

The formal request must include a detailed account of having completed the *parivāsa* and so forth, thereby requesting the six-night period; this is called "granting by way of increase" because this legal procedure is granted as an addition to the preceding [period].

Second, when one originally commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense without any intention to conceal it and discloses it to others, one need only directly grant the *mānatva* rite; this is not called "granting an increased [penance]."
Now, since the root of the precepts is difficult to attain, the superior giving is clarified.

Fourth, "Having completed the practice of *mānatva*": during the period of practice, one is deprived of thirty-five matters and must provide offerings to visiting monks; this is largely the same as the concealment [of offenses], as explained in detail in the *Pārājika-kaṇḍa* (Concealment Khandhaka).

5. Regarding the phrase "the offense of this bhikṣu must be expiated before an assembly of twenty monks": once the six-night penance has been completed, the bhikṣu who committed the offense should seek out a full assembly of twenty pure monks. He should formally report the performance of the *parivāsa* (probation) and the completion of the six nights as the petition for his request. He makes three requests before the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants him the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for the rite of absolution from the offense.

Of the five stages mentioned above, there are only three formal procedures (*dharma*): namely, concealment (*praticchādana*), the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*), and the restoration from guilt (*āpattivyutthāna*).
As for the previous mention that "there may be four formal procedures," this refers to such methods as the *yathācitta* (treatment according to the original offense).

For example, suppose one has committed an offense subject to concealment (*pārājika*) and has already undergone the *parivāsa* probation for one hundred days; having requested the *parivāsa* from the Saṃgha and completed ten days, one suddenly commits another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. The preceding ten days are then nullified, and one must begin the probation anew, observing it for the full original period.
If that relative commits an offense, one must separately request it from the Saṃgha according to whether it was concealed or not, and it must likewise be practiced.
However, regarding the new and old offenses, at the time of requesting them, whether they are combined or separated—whether practiced together or separately—there is no hindrance.

Regarding the "previously mentioned six or seven": among the five stages, or within the concealment (*paryuṣita*), adding the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction to the original day) constitutes one set of six; or, adding the *mūlāpakarṣa* to the six nights constitutes another set of six; or, adding the *mūlāpakarṣa* to both the concealment and the six nights results in seven.
The principles of opening and closing, as well as commonality and distinction, are likewise applicable throughout.
The third section of the preceding ritual for repentance is hereby concluded.
Below follows the fourth section, which explains the fault of having too few monks present.

Therefore, the text states: "If even one person is missing so that the assembly does not number twenty, the offense of this bhikṣu cannot be removed. This means the offense of that bhikṣu cannot be expiated.

However, for the concealment of offenses over six nights, one is cleared of the offense on the day it originally occurred; as for the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*), both the legal procedure and the ritual itself are performed by the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations).

Regarding the assembly required: for the first three [grave offenses], only a quorum of four monks is required to perform the rite, whereas for the single rite of clearing the offense, the quorum is restricted to twenty monks.
As explained in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vyākhyāyukti*) and its commentary by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha:
if one person is missing—if there is simply a deficiency in number—the principle is that it is insufficient;
even if the count is made up by including those who have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*) or nuns, it is still termed insufficient.
As stated in the Vinaya:
twenty-eight types of persons do not constitute a quorum for the Saṃgha.

To summarize this briefly in verse: "The remaining [cases] involve formal accusation, reconciliation, and difficulties; through supernatural concealment or departure, one is unable to attend the assembly. A detailed exposition is not afforded here."
From this point downward is the fifth section, which demonstrates that the Saṃgha may possess faults; thus the text states, "The bhikṣus may also reprove [him].
Generally speaking, when one speaks of deliverance, one must distinguish between what is correct and what is not;
if one does not understand the Dharma, one will be reproved by the Sages and incur a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅) offense.
From this point downward, the sixth section concludes the formation of what accords with the Dharma;
thus the text says, "This is the proper time.
This means that while one observes the faults of listening [to worldly matters], one acts in accordance with the teachings; this is what constitutes being timely.
The details for examining and upholding these [rules] should be understood as previously stated.
From here on, the third major section concerns the two indeterminate offenses (*aniyata*).
This section is also divided into three parts:
First, the teaching upon which it is based; second, the enumeration of its names and characteristics; third, the conclusion and careful retention thereof.
The first section is self-evident.
Within the enumeration of names and characteristics, the first is the precept on the *anavasthāpya* (probation) for concealment.
The text consists of three sections:
first, the person who may commit the offense; second, the discernment of the indeterminate characteristics; and third, the conclusion regarding the name "indeterminate.
Within the second section, the discernment of characteristics, there are four subsections:

First, regarding the phrase "sitting and speaking improper words with a woman alone in a secluded, concealed place suitable for sexual intercourse," there are three meanings, which are termed "undetermined" (aniyata).
First, regarding "in a secluded place": this refers to the locus where the commission of an offense originates; therefore, it is termed "indeterminate" with respect to its origin.
It is like parents seeing their wicked son committing an unrighteous act in a village lane; this village lane is the locus from which the commission of the offense originates.
Second, regarding this passage, "Furthermore, one sees a bhikṣu sitting alone with a woman, speaking unwholesome words," there are two further meanings:
first, concerning the preliminary conditions for the bhikṣu’s commission of an offense, these conditions are not fixed.
Secondly, regarding the accusation based on one's abiding faith, the matters perceived by the Noble Woman (Āryā) are not fixed in their specific characteristics.

The Vinaya text provisionally relies upon the etiquette of sitting together; however, according to the commentary on the *Vidyāmātrasiddhi-śāstra* (Mingliao lun) by Paramārtha, if [the act] occurs while walking, standing, or lying down, it likewise falls within the scope of an offense.
2. Regarding the phrase, "A laywoman who abides in faith—a noble laywoman who has attained indestructible faith—is said to 'abide in faith.

Within the three dharmas, she speaks of each individual dharma, even down to a *pāyattika* offense," this means that the noble woman, relying on the circumstances of the prior commission of the offense and the phenomena she has witnessed, comes before the Saṃgha to speak.
Regarding its characteristics, there are three types, such as the *pārājika* and so forth; however, upon examining the various schools, they themselves have three different explanations.
First, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the phenomena observed are cited collectively as a whole; thus, that text states: "What is the *aniyata*?"

One merely sees women coming and going, sitting or standing; one does not see them engaging in sexual intercourse, taking human life, touching women, killing grass, eating past noon, or drinking alcohol. For this reason, it is called "indeterminate."

Second, according to the commentary on the *Vyākhyāyukti* by Paramārtha, regarding the phenomena observed, only those involving sexual desire across all categories of offenses (*pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*) are cited.
Thus, that commentary states: "If one has already engaged in sexual intercourse and subsequently sits together [with the woman], it is a *pārājika*;
if one has already completed the act of touching, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
If one desires sexual contact, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one merely sits with a defiled mind, it is a *pāyattika*;
if there is no defiled mind, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Third, based on this *Caturvarga-vinaya* text, only three offenses are mentioned; the Vinaya does not state that there are further offenses remaining. Thus, among those involving defilement, only the coarse aspects of the offenses are subsumed under the "undetermined" category for investigation and examination.

As for the others that are subtle, fearing they would be too numerous and cumbersome, they are not examined here; one should instead allow the individual to confess them according to their own account.

3. Regarding the phrase, "The bhikṣu sitting here says of himself: 'I have committed this offense,' up to 'a pāyattika,'" it means that during the preliminary proceedings, having observed the signs of the matter and reported them to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha interrogated him and established these three types of offenses; therefore, the appropriate disciplinary measures are determined according to these three.

4. Regarding the statement, "The bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma as stated by a laywoman (upāsikā) who abides in faith": since the person in question refused to confess their offense when interrogated and could not be made to admit it, one must therefore hold them as guilty based on what was said by the noble woman. The Saṃgha should then deal with them according to the legal procedure for the place of the offense (*yathāvadāna*), namely, through the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Thus, it is said that "the bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma."

There are thirty-five matters to be set aside, which lead to the determination of the actual location of the offense and the legal procedure for that location; these are explained in detail in the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Chapter on the Extinction of Disputes) within the Vinaya.

Since this person refuses to acknowledge the location of the offense, it is precisely the fault of their indeterminate state that must be addressed—this being exactly the transgression prevented by this precept.
The faults herein regarding the intention are threefold: first, being in a secluded and concealed place that serves as the occasion for the offense;
second, speaking improper words to a woman, which constitutes the characteristic of the occasion for committing the offense;
and third, failing to provide a definitive account when questioned by the Saṃgha, which is the fault of one's own disposition.
Since all these are prevented by this very precept, one commits the offense of silence and falsehood in total when questioned three times.

In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the term "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) is explained according to its etymological derivation; thus, the text states: "It is indeterminate because it is the cause of various offenses; therefore, it is called 'indeterminate'."

Furthermore, regarding that which is not cited, one must interrogate [the opponent] to establish certainty, thereby resolving the indeterminate; thus, that text states: "In this context, the various offenses are indeterminate.
The masters of antiquity were deeply ignorant of this, and their extensive discourse was verbose; failing to perceive the correct principle, they were unable to provide a complete exposition.

These two indeterminate offenses are restricted to cases where a noble woman (āryā) accuses a monk of a fault and reports it to the Saṃgha for formal interrogation; this is because a noble person would rather die than speak falsely.
If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) makes the accusation, no interrogation is conducted.
The second [category], the Indeterminate (aniyata), also consists of three sections:
first, the possibility of an offense; second, the definition of the indeterminate characteristics; and third, the formal conclusion of the name "Indeterminate.
Regarding the second section, the definition of the characteristics, there are also four subsections:
1. "Sitting in the open with a woman and speaking unwholesome words" refers to the factual circumstances observed as the origin of the offense.
2. Based on the aforementioned factual circumstances, one approaches the Saṃgha and speaks of them.
However, only two offenses are mentioned because, in an exposed location, sexual misconduct is impossible.

Third, regarding the preliminary stage: having observed the signs of the incident and reported it to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha interrogated him and established these two offenses; therefore, he was dealt with accordingly.
4. If the person in question conceals their offense, one should trust the noble woman and maintain that they have committed an offense.
The determination of the locus of the offense and the principles of its treatment are explained in detail according to the preceding sections.
Regarding the third section on "having formally concluded and carefully maintained [the rule]," it is as stated in the text.
In this context, it is not determined which offense requires confession; therefore, it cannot be classified within the formal categories [of the Prātimokṣa].
Furthermore, there is no textual passage concerning its confession.

Commentary on the *Bhikṣu-Prātimokṣa* in Four Sections, Scroll Lower, composed by the Śramaṇa Dingbin of the State-Sanctifying Monastery on Mount Song.
From here below begins the fourth major section: the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas. The text is further divided as follows:
The third [category] should be understood as before.
*Naiḥsargika* (ni-sa-gi) is translated here as "exhaustive relinquishment.
*Pāyattika* (po-yi-ti) is translated here as "falling" (*pātayantika*).
This means that committing this offense drags one down into the three evil realms; because this refers to the general name [of the category], it is called "falling" (pāyattika).

If one commits this falling offense, one must first relinquish the material object and subsequently repent for the falling offense; therefore, it is called "relinquishment-and-falling" (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
However, when the thirty precepts are subdivided, there are actually thirty-two precepts; that is to say, two precepts concerning the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-bathing robe) are combined into one.
As for these two, the first is begging for it prematurely, and the second is using it prematurely.
Furthermore, the two rules regarding the "immediate gift of robes" (*akālacīvara*) are combined into one: first, receiving it before the prescribed time;
second, keeping it after the prescribed time. Together with the other twenty-eight rules, they total thirty-two.
However, regarding the violation of the thirty-two precepts, there are four major categories:
first, giving the property to another; second, completing the repentance for the offense; third, returning the property; and fourth, failing to return it, thereby incurring the full penalty.
Regarding the minor variations in the intermediate rules of training, one should consult the relevant passages.
The name "Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" (Forfeiture) is established based on the first two categories.
However, upon examining the prescriptions for forfeiture, it is because one possesses items in an improper manner and generates greed through their use that forfeiture is mandated.
There are briefly six categories of unlawful possession (*adharmika-parigraha*):
first, unlawful possession characterized by lack of contentment despite having already acquired [requisites], such as possessing the five "long" items;
second, unlawful possession characterized by violating the teachings and lacking necessary resources, such as being separated from one's robes for two nights.
Third, engaging in unrighteous conduct that invites ridicule and brings disgrace, such as taking robes from a bhikṣuṇī, washing robes, carrying wool, or carding wool;
fourth, indulging in unrighteous attachment to clothing, such as begging for robes from a single householder or encouraging two householders to increase the price and have them weave finer cloth;
fifth, harassing others through unrighteous and excessive demands for robes or seizing their robes.

The six [offenses] involving greed for storage, obstructing, procrastination, illegal acts, and exceeding moderation; selling the five [kinds of goods], spreading out two kinds of precious objects, begging for bowls and begging for thread, the rainy-season robe, giving what was urgently offered before its time, and diverting property belonging to the Saṃgha.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, carrying wool over a long distance gives rise to illness; for now, this shall be subsumed under the category of "inciting derision.
There are six types of improper wealth that cannot be used again; because they are enjoyed with a mind of greed, they must be relinquished through formal renunciation (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Question:

Within the *pācittiya* offenses, using wealth also falls under the six types of misconduct; since it is still used with a mind of greed, why is "giving it away" (*nissaggiya*) not prescribed as the remedy? Answer:
Among the thirty types of material wealth, two are capable of long-term storage and two are essential for sustaining the body.
Once one falls into the six non-leavings, these are mostly used out of greed; therefore, one must establish the forfeiture rule to discipline the greedy mind.
Regarding items that may be kept individually: first, those that cannot be stored for long periods, such as separate meals;
second, those that are not essential for sustaining the body, such as white garments.

Therefore, one falls into six kinds of non-virtue; these mostly give rise to other delusions rather than much greed. Since greed is not being treated [as the primary issue], why must it be specifically restrained and abandoned?

Furthermore, consider the case of taking more than three bowls of food: once one has already finished eating and then carries away more than three, one simply cannot eat again on that very day; this is not the arising of greed.
If one wishes to remain, one cannot endure it for long.
This merely causes harm and distress to the donor through delusion; since there is no greed to be remedied, why should there be a need to establish a rule for relinquishing it?
Matters such as eating apart from the assembly may cause distress to the Sangha; all such cases should be explained by analogy.

As for high beds, lay clothing, and the like, these are maintained due to ignorant teachings; since their use gives rise to much delusion and indolence, and one does not even govern one's greed, what need is there to speak of renouncing them?
Question:
Since a cotton mattress has been torn and destroyed, it should be treated like a needle case; why, then, is it classified as an item to be relinquished (*niḥsargika*)? Answer:
A small object such as a hypodermic needle, because it leads to distraction, is neither subject to the abandonment of greed nor does it enter into equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Question:
Since ginger used for food cannot be stored for long, why is it included among objects of equanimity?
Answer: Within the precept against buying and selling, the trading of food is not restricted; therefore, it is included in the forfeiture along with other items.
Question:
Question: Since one observes the three types of concealment (*paryavasthāna*), and greed (*rāga*) ought to arise [in response], why does it not enter into equanimity (*upekṣā*)? Answer:

A dwelling is a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*) and not an essential or urgent necessity; thus, greed is also slight in its significance. Should other difficulties arise, they should be explained according to this principle.
The preceding questions and answers have exhausted the principles without exception.
According to this, regarding the thirty types of wealth: first, there is the fault of the moment of transgression, such as falling into the six non-allowable acts;
second, there is the fault after having committed the transgression, such as the *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) incurred upon using them.
Regarding the ninety types of wealth, there is only a *thullaccaya* offense at the time of transgression, yet no fault of having already committed the offense.

Among the five "excesses" within the aforementioned six unlawful acts, not only does one commit the offense by using them greedily, but it is also fundamentally because of insatiability that they constitute a fault.

Therefore, according to the tradition handed down from antiquity, when relinquishing [the extra robe], one must necessarily stay overnight before being permitted to return, in order to sever the insatiable desire for accumulation.

Thus, the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that once the confession for relinquishing the long robe is completed, if this bhikṣu has a matter of necessity and wishes to travel far away, he should be asked:
"To whom shall you give this robe?"

Following those instructions, he gave it to him, saying: "You must not sit down immediately; you should return directly. Therefore, he entrusted it to a bhikṣu who was a friend of the recipient; that friendly bhikṣu stayed overnight before returning it.
Now, examining this in detail according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, even if one has spent the night, as long as the covetous mind has not ceased, one has not yet regained [the robe].
Therefore, the fourth fascicle of that treatise states: "If one relinquishes the robe on that very day but repents on that same day, yet the desire for the robe is not severed."

Even up to one month, if the robe sought arrives, or if an unexpected robe arrives, these are all considered "continuous" because the intention to keep them continues in succession; therefore, regarding the previous robe, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, examining that treatise in detail, it requires an overnight stay and, moreover, a mental severance. Thus, the text states:

"If one has already relinquished the robe on this day and confessed the transgression, and on that very day effects a mental severance, then even if the conditions for seeking a robe arise again on a subsequent day, they do not constitute a continuous succession because of the intervening mental severance."
The *Shu* states: "Since this is the case for extra robes (*dīrgha-cīvara*), it stands to reason that the same principle applies to all other extra precepts (*dīrgha-śīla*).

Once the five types of 'extra' items have been excluded, when one relinquishes any other remaining precepts through confession (*pratideśanā*), they may all be returned to their original owners while still seated."

If one possesses five long robes and relinquishes them, yet has not yet recovered them by this day, and then takes a nun’s robe or similar garment which is immediately returned, at the moment it enters one's hands, it becomes tainted by the previous long robes and thus constitutes an offense of "excess. Therefore, these cases are treated together, and the items must be returned after having been kept overnight.
If a dharma is easily accomplished, it should be relinquished at a different time.
The Vinaya text does not mention the dyeing of robes or bowls; although a nun’s robe and bowl may sometimes be relinquished together, the robe is returned immediately and is not stained by the bowl.
Reflect upon this accordingly.
First, we shall explain the precept against keeping extra robes (*atirekacīvara*).
The text consists of four points:
First, the person who commits the offense;
second, the exclusion of conditions for exemption, meaning that which constitutes no offense.

Regarding the phrase "the robes are finished," if one carefully examines the intent of the Vinaya, it refers to the completion of the earlier *anvārohaṇa* (rainy-season retreat) at the end of the month of Kārttika, or the acceptance of the *kāṭhina* robe.

In the fifth month, the permission to make robes begins; at this time, it is not necessary to perform the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification), and one does not incur the offense of keeping an extra robe (*dīrgha-āpatti*).
Once this one-month period beyond the fifth month has passed, the permission to make robes concludes; therefore, it is said that "the making of robes is finished."
