Therefore, in the account of the origin (*nidāna*) of the precept concerning eating in a separate group, it says: "After the monks had completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they made robes during the month of Kārttika.
The Buddha consequently permitted that during the month of making robes, one may eat in a separate group."

Furthermore, according to the *Prakīrṇaka* on the rule regarding eating in a group, the commentary explaining the characteristics states: "At the time of making robes" refers to the period from the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony—lasting one month when the *kāṭhina* robe-privilege has not been spread, and five months when it has been spread—up until the point where even a single "horse-tooth" stitch has been made upon the robe.
It is clearly understood that this also generally refers to the opening of the period for making robes in the fifth month.
From this point until one month after the fifth month, all such periods are termed "the robe-making is finished.
Therefore, the explanatory text on the characteristics of the *dīrghacīvara* (extra robe) precept states: "'The robe-making is finished' refers to the three robes (*tricīvara*)."
The *Shu* says: "This refers to having finished making the three robes.
Question:
One may also make extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) during the one-month or five-month periods; why is it mentioned here only in relation to the three robes?
Answer: It is named after its most prominent feature. Master Nanshan said:
Regarding the statement in the three subsequent precepts that "the robes are finished": this refers to the robes being finished.

This means the material and substance for the three robes are sufficient; anything beyond that constitutes an extra garment. Now, to examine the intent behind keeping them: one may keep them with the intention of making the three robes, pending their completion.
If one has the intention to keep [the robes] but does not plan to make them into the three robes (tricīvara), why wait until they are complete?

Next, regarding the phrase "the robes are finished": this means that the three robes have been completed and accepted for formal possession; otherwise, there would be the fault of being separated from them overnight.

Regarding the later statement, "the robes are finished": this means that the material for the three robes has been completed as a single unit. If one does not make the robes or fails to perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification), it constitutes an offense.

Now, examining the previous point regarding the meaning of the one-month and five-month periods, these apply universally to the three types of precepts, because they equally obtain the five kinds of benefits.
The meaning of the five benefits is as explained below.
If one follows the interpretation of the Nanshan [Vinaya], the three precepts each have their own distinct scope; one may maintain both views as appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "the kaṭhina robe has been removed," this refers to the conclusion of the earlier retreat on the sixteenth day of the seventh month.

If there is a donor who offers one of the three robes from among his own set, it shall be accepted on that very day. On that same day, a formal motion with a subsequent proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) shall be made to appoint one person, and another formal motion with a subsequent proclamation shall be made to entrust the robe to that person.
The person entrusted with the robe shall take this single garment and, proceeding before the assembly of monks, kneel on their right knee and present it to them.

Any monk who wishes to accept it shall grasp the garment with his hand and receive it by reciting the prescribed formula; this must continue in order until the lowest seat has received it, completing the sequence.
The person to whom it has been entrusted shall, from this time forth until the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, always remain within the boundary and guard this single robe.
This robe which is thus guarded is called *kaṭhina* in Sanskrit, which here means "the firm and solid robe."

This robe is composed of solid and substantial wealth; furthermore, it causes the donor to receive solid and substantial retribution, and it causes the Saṃgha to obtain five kinds of solid and substantial meritorious benefits:
first, one may keep an extra robe (*aticīvara*) without declaring it pure (*asuddhika*) and thus not incur the offense of keeping an extra robe;
second, among the three robes, one may leave any one behind without incurring the offense of being separated from them overnight.
Third, one may receive food passed from person to person;
fourth, one may receive food from a separate group;
fifth, one need not announce one's intention before or after entering a village for a meal.

Furthermore, because the person guarding the robe does not accept the five privileges, but guards it with firm integrity without staying overnight outside the boundary, thereby benefiting others, it is called the "firm and solid robe" (kaṭhina) and is also called the "robe of merit" (guṇa-kaṭhina).

For those who have received these benefits, during the five-month period, should any of the eight conditions arise—at whatever time they may occur—the moment one such condition is encountered, the five benefits are forfeited; this forfeiture constitutes their "withdrawal. Therefore, it is said that "the *kaṭhina* robe has been withdrawn," meaning that after its withdrawal, one must perform the ritual of *śuddhika-vyavahāra* (purification by declaration).
Regarding the third phrase, "One may keep an extra robe for ten days without performing the *viśuddhi* (purification) rite," this means that keeping it is permitted within the limit.
To extend the period would lead to negligence, while to shorten it would cause fatigue; therefore, one must complete the *viśuddhi* rite within ten days.

Regarding clothing and materials, regardless of whether they are new or old, inner or outer garments, as soon as they reach the measurement of one chi, six cun, and eight fen, one must perform the ritual of "declared purity" (śuddhi-vyākaraṇa).
One who performs this rite of purity demonstrates a mind of contentment and avoids the notion of ownership.
Regarding the fourth phrase, "If [the period] exceeds ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense," this establishes the transgression.
According to the Vinaya texts, if one obtains robes day by day within the ten-day period, upon reaching the eleventh day, all such acquisitions constitute an offense.

Although the nine days following have not yet exceeded the limit, because the first day already exceeded the permitted period for possession, all nine days are subject to the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
The detailed explanation is as found in the Vinaya.
Having committed this offense, one ought to perform repentance (*pratideśanā*).
Regarding the method of repentance, it shall be briefly analyzed through three sections:

first, clarifying the presence or absence and the magnitude of the accumulated offenses; second, distinguishing the sequence and stages for repenting the offenses; and third, correctly explaining the ritual for relinquishing and restoring [the precepts] through repentance.
First, regarding the determination of their number: they may comprise ten offenses.
First, those such as the *atirekacīvara* (extra robe) and *nissaggiya* (separation from the robe), where the substance of the object is currently present and may be subject to forfeiture.
2. When extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) and so forth have already been used up or destroyed, one simply confesses the offense.
3. Concealing a *thullaccaya* offense constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
4. If this *thullaccaya* and *dukkaṭa* are successively concealed night after night, one incurs further *dukkaṭas*.
5. To wear it is an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
6. To conceal this very [offense] is an offense of wrongdoing.
7. To conceal this very [act of concealing] is an offense of wrongdoing.
8. When the Saṃgha recites the precepts, if one commits an offense and remains silent when questioned twice or thrice, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
9. If one conceals this very offense, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

10. If one follows along with the concealment of this very offense, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Among these ten offenses, whether one possesses one, two, or more, one should confess them according to the specific matter.
Second, regarding the explanation of the sequence and stages for repenting transgressions: one should first relinquish material wealth and subsequently repent for all offenses.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "First relinquish objects, and only thereafter clearly explain the extinction of offenses. (End of citation from the treatise.)
"Current practice is entirely consistent with this.
The sequence for the confession of offenses should be divided into three stages:
first, one must confess the concealment (*paryuṣita*) and the transgression of concealing it (*paryuṣitāpatti*). This follows the text of the *Pudgalavastu* (or *Pudgalakhandhaka*)."

Since the two root *pārājika* offenses and the offense of silent falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*) differ in their essential natures, there is no single remedy capable of eliminating them simultaneously; therefore, it is necessary to further distinguish between the *pārājika* and *sthūlātyaya* categories.
Therefore, one first confesses the two types of *duṣkṛta*—the *mūla-duṣkṛta* and the *tūṣṇīmbhāva-duṣkṛta*—and only thereafter confesses the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, thereby establishing three stages:
in the first stage, one confesses the six categories of *duṣkṛta* associated with each of the concealments (*chādana*) and subsequent concealments (*anupraticchādana*) of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
in the second stage, one confesses the two categories of *duṣkṛta* associated with the *mūla-duṣkṛta* and *tūṣṇīmbhāva-duṣkṛta*.
The third is the *saṃtati-pāyattika*.
At present, all ritual practices follow this pattern.
Examining the various Vinayas and śāstras, there are two types of confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense:
The first is repentance through self-reproach; the second is repentance before another.
Since these various auspicious signs are now so significant, they should all be repented of through confession before another.
Third, regarding the formal determination of the method for relinquishing and restoring [the precepts], it is divided into two sections:
First is the application of the mind through making a vow; second is the formal procedure for relinquishing and confessing transgressions.

Regarding the initial application of the mind, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states: "In all cases where one speaks of *vipaśyanā*, having first discerned the causes of the offense, its origination, its essential nature, and its faults, one should properly disclose them to a person worthy of trust and properly seek to receive the protective remedy."
The *Shu* states: "To 'tiśāna' (tishena) is translated as 'to reveal' (*pradarśana*), and it is also called 'confessing offenses'; this is precisely what repentance (*pratideśanā*) is.
As for the 'causes of offense,' these may be due to various afflictions (*kleśa*), such as greed and so forth."
Regarding "conditioned origination" (pratyaya), it refers to how an offense is incurred due to such things as eating at improper times or drinking alcohol.
Regarding "essential characteristics" (lakṣaṇa), it refers to identifying that "this is a saṃghāvaśeṣa" or "this is a pāyattika," and so forth.
Regarding faults: for one who commits an offense, there are five faults:

first, it can obstruct *nirvāṇa*; second, it obstructs the path to *nirvāṇa*; third, it engenders lack of faith in others; fourth, it increases one's own evil karma; and fifth, it brings about retribution in the evil realms.
Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes the full comprehension of the time, place, and other circumstances in which the offense was committed.

As for the term "a person worthy of trust," it refers to one who possesses a kind heart; because such a person will not, upon being told of one's offense, turn around and report one's faults to others, they are said to be "worthy of trust."
Furthermore, because that person’s observance of the precepts is pure and upright, they are said to be trustworthy.

Now, in this degenerate age, those who are bright and pure are difficult to find; for this reason, practitioners of antiquity took those who had not committed the same offense as the object of their confession.
Now the Tripitaka Master says:
"In Western practice, 'counteracting' (pratipakṣa) refers to different offenses; it requires taking up a counteraction for an offense of a different category.
One who seeks to receive the protective power of the counteraction first loses the mind of that protective counteraction; now, by permanently severing its continuity, one is once again receiving it."
Second, regarding the formal determination of relinquishing, repentance, and so forth, there are four sections:
first, relinquishing wealth; second, repenting offenses; third, returning wealth; and fourth, the offense incurred for not returning it.
First, we shall distinguish the meaning of the offense regarding extra robes; the rest may be understood by analogy with this.

First, let us clarify the relinquishment of the material object: according to the Vinaya texts, it is mandatory that all members of the community assemble; it is not permitted to relinquish the object to another group separately.
The object to which it is offered may be the Saṃgha as a whole, or it may be two or three individuals, or even a single person; in all such cases, there is no impediment.
However, if it is to be relinquished to the Saṃgha, it must necessarily be restricted to within the boundaries of the ritual precinct (*karmabhūmi*).
Whether it be with two, three, or even down to one person, this applies universally within the naturally established dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
For now, we shall address the ease of relinquishing [the precepts] to a single individual; the rest shall be analyzed in detail elsewhere.
The *pātra-pratigrahaṇa-śīla* (the vow of begging for a bowl) must specifically be undertaken in the presence of the Saṃgha; this will be explained further below.

At present, the performance of this rite is mostly conducted either on the *śīlākṣetra* (precepts field) or within the *prakṛti-sīmā* (natural boundary). Regarding the three types of *prakṛti-sīmā*, they have already been distinguished above.

If the person one is approaching is of high status, one should maintain proper decorum: baring the right shoulder, removing the leather sandals, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, and holding the robe with the hands. If the person is of lower status, the prostration at their feet is omitted; one should simply say:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!"
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept one long robe, two or three robes, etc.—the same applies when referring to the number accordingly.
If the items are so numerous that they cannot be distinguished individually, one may say 'many';
if they can be counted, one must state the specific number."

If it is a bolt of cloth, one must specify the length of the material; for those who commit the offense by dyeing it on the ninth day after the tenth day has passed, this phrase "impure gift" need not be used, as they commit one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), or two, three, and so forth.
"Now, I offer this robe or this wealth to the Venerable One; [this is] the first declaration.
Regarding the second confession for the expiation of offenses: the distinctions between *thullaccaya* and *pācittiya* are divided into three categories, as has already been explained above.

First, to distinguish the six categories of *duṣkṛta* offenses involving concealment (*mrakṣa*) and subsequent concealment: within these, there are two further points. First, one should invite a confession master (*pratideśanā-ācārya*) who has not committed the same offense, as previously explained; then, assuming the proper deportment as before, one says orally:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!"

I, Bhikṣu [Name], now request the Venerable One to act as my witness for the confession of a *duṣkṛta* offense. May the Venerable One act as my witness for the confession of this *duṣkṛta* offense out of compassion. (Recite once.)
He replied, “So be it.
Next, for the ritual of repenting one’s transgressions, he spoke as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept an extra robe for more than ten days without having performed the ritual of 'impure giving,' thereby committing one offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."

Furthermore, due to wearing and using [the garment], one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) for the robe, as well as an offense of *duṣkṛta*. Whether one does not remember the number or remembers the number, one should state it according to the count, such as "one," "two," and so forth.

Furthermore, during the recitation of the precepts by the Saṃgha, after two locations and three inquiries, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta* for remaining silent while having transgressed, or for claiming to remember when one does not, or for claiming to remember according to the number [of times].

Once these fundamental offenses of the three stages have been committed, if one fails to confess each of them and instead conceals them throughout the night, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta*, whether one does not remember the number or claims to remember according to the number.
Passing the night in succession, one further commits the *duṣkṛta* offense of concealment (*paticchādana*).

Whether one does not remember the number of days or counts them accordingly, herein lie six grades of *duṣkṛta* offenses for concealment and subsequent concealment. I now confess these before the Venerable One; I dare not conceal them.
"I pray that the Venerable One will remember my single recitation. He should reply:
"Reproach yourself and give rise to a sense of weary detachment."
The offender replies, "So be it. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it is also acceptable to say, "I shall bear this upon my head.
Second, for the confession of the two categories of *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses), there is no need to request a presiding master (*sāṃghika*) again, as one has already been requested previously.
The ritual formula is as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept an extra robe for more than ten days without having performed the *viśuddhi-dāna* (purificatory gift), thereby committing one offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."

Having committed this offense, if one wears or uses clothing or property that should be forfeited due to an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, one commits an offense of *duṣkṛta*; whether one does not recall the number of times it was worn or uses it according to the number.

Furthermore, during the *poṣadha* recitation of the Saṃgha, if one passes through two places or three gates while committing the offense of silent falsehood (*tūṣṇīmbhāva-mṛṣāvāda*), one commits an offense of *duṣkṛta*; whether one does not recall the number of times it occurred or acts according to the number.
"Now, I confess and repent before the Venerable One; the detailed explanation is the same as before.
Third, the formal confession of the root *pāyattika* offense.
Within this, one must first request a confessor (*kṣamāpaka*) who has not committed the same offense, and perform the ritual with the following words:
“Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, the bhikṣu [name], now request the Venerable sir to act as the presiding master for the confession of a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. May the Venerable sir, out of compassion, act as the presiding master for my confession of the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. (Recite this three times.)
He replied, “So be it.
Next, he performed the formal repentance for his transgressions.
The Vinaya Master of the Southern Mountain said:
"One should briefly explain the Dharma.
He then addressed them, saying:
The Buddha said:
"I have established precepts for my disciples so that they would rather die than transgress them.

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 15: 'A person who breaks the precepts and falsely consumes the offerings of the faithful finds that the alms-bowl they hold is actually a vessel of molten copper, and the robes they wear are sheets of glowing iron; furthermore, because of their violation of the precepts, they receive the body of a hairless insect or one that feeds on excrement.'"
"Thus, [the instruction] consists of only three or five sentences according to the individual's capacity.

If, however, one is dull-witted such that their mind remains unmoved even upon hearing these harsh words, it is not necessary to show them the path, nor should one accept their repentance, because [their afflictions] would continue."
Regarding the words for confession, one should recite them with the proper ritual form as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!

I, Bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept a piece of extra robe-cloth for more than ten days without having performed the *aviśuddha-dāna* (purificatory gift), thereby committing one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
This robe has already been relinquished to the Venerable One or relinquished to another; it should be stated that it has been relinquished to [Name].
This *pāyattika* offense, I now confess and repent before the Venerable One, not daring to conceal it.
To repent brings peace and happiness; not to repent brings no peace or happiness.
I recall my transgression and disclose it; knowing it, I do not conceal it.
May the Venerable One bear in mind that my body of pure precepts is complete, having fulfilled the three proclamations of the pure *poṣadha*.
One should say: "Reproach yourself and give rise to revulsion. He replies:
"So be it," he replied; or he said,
"I shall receive it upon my head."

Third, regarding the returning of property: if there is a separation by one *nakṣatra* (lunar mansion), it shall be returned the following day; it is simply handed over by hand without any further words or phrases.

When the Sangha returns it, the formal procedure of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion with one proclamation) is performed. Once it has been received, one should declare it as pure (*viśuddhi*) and keep it in accordance with the Dharma.
The words for declaring purity (*śuddhi-uddeśa*) are recited by all;

as for the fourth, the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), the Vinaya states that one must confess before two or three people or the Sangha, and because the procedure is somewhat complex and difficult, it is not detailed here.
Second is the precept against staying overnight separated from one’s robe.

The original intent behind establishing this precept was for those who have newly received the ordination; if they were to expand upon it further, they would not suddenly understand it. Therefore, for now, one may simply keep the robe with oneself and it shall not constitute an offense. If one wishes to gain thorough understanding, one should seek out extensive study; for the time being, I shall provide only a brief explanation.
"Except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha" means: if one is ill and the robes are heavy, and there is a necessary reason to travel, one should request three times from the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha shall then perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to permit [the monk] to retain one robe from among his three robes.
Although one may pass through the dawn (aruṇa), one does not commit the offense of staying apart from one’s robe; this is explained in detail in the Vinaya.
As for the rules regarding the making and maintaining of robes, there is no leisure to elaborate upon them here.

Third, the rule concerning the replacement of old tri-cīvara with new materials as they arrive during the month is called the "Month-Waning Robe" (yuèwàng yī) by Nanshan; the old name was the "One-Month Robe Rule" (yīyuè yī jiè). Since both meanings were somewhat obscure, it has been revised.
The five phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
first, the person who may commit the offense;
second, the exclusion of the exceptional circumstances, because at the time of making robes there is no fault of exceeding the prescribed length.
Third, urging [the donor] to complete it quickly.

Regarding the phrase "obtaining out-of-season robes" (*akālacīvara*): this refers to obtaining newly cut cloth outside of the one-month or five-month period for making robes; such is termed an "out-of-season robe."
Having returned from this untimely period of ten days, it is because this is always permitted that there is no need for haste in its completion.
Upon reaching the tenth day, if the funds are sufficient, one should complete it immediately;
if they are insufficient, it is permitted to extend until the eleventh day, and if they are sufficient on the eleventh, one should complete it immediately.

If it is insufficient, one may extend the period until the twelfth day, continuing in this manner up to the twenty-ninth day; in all these cases, there is the principle that the robe is completed on that very day. Therefore, it is said that "the robe is quickly completed."
Furthermore, it says, "If [the provisions] are sufficient, that is well," which refers to the twenty types of wholesome conditions for the completion [of the robe].
Fourth, this clearly explains the continuation of the procurement of new materials, which may extend up to one month.

Regarding the scriptural statement, "If it is insufficient, one may keep it for one month," this means that from the tenth day until the twenty-ninth day—spanning twenty days—if the requisites remain unfulfilled, one is permitted to keep them until the thirtieth day without incurring the offense of *atireka* (excess). Therefore, it is said that one may keep them for one month.
The text states, "For the sake of fulfillment," which means there are twenty consecutive acts performed for the sake of fulfillment.
Fifth, the offense of keeping [the item] after the transgression has been incurred.

Upon reaching the thirtieth day, regardless of whether new wealth is sufficient or insufficient, one must immediately perform the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity), or give it away to others, or make it into robes and so forth.
If the thirtieth day passes without doing so, one invariably incurs an offense; hence it is said thus.

According to the traditional interpretation of the meaning of this precept handed down from antiquity, those who practice the higher path maintain only the three robes; when these old garments become worn out and decayed, they are merely fit for formal observance but no longer suitable for actual wear.
Now, regarding the acquisition of new wealth that one does not intend to perform the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification), it is permitted to wait until it reaches the maximum limit of one month.
Now, upon closer examination, I fear this may not necessarily be the case.
If a practitioner of superior conduct does not wish to perform the *śuddhika*, how could one suddenly compel them to do so on the thirtieth day, thereby undermining their superior resolve?

Therefore, it is known that if one designates the mind [of the recipient] as a substitute for an old robe, one may keep it for an extended period; this does not distinguish between those of superior conduct.
Fourth, the precept concerning taking a robe from a nun who is not a relative.
"Relatives" must be those within seven generations of one's parents; if one washes for them beyond this, it is not an offense.
Furthermore, a precept-receiving disciple is also considered a non-relative.
Fifth is the precept against having a nun who is not a relative wash one's used robes.
The three *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules concerning washing, dyeing, and beating [a robe] are incurred even down to a single instance of wearing it oneself; this is what constitutes "old.
Sixth: The precept against begging for robes from the household of a non-relative layperson.
This constitutes an offense regarding robes of improper measure.
Except when one's robes have been stolen by bandits and so forth, there is no offense in begging for them.
Seventh: The precept against receiving robes beyond what is sufficient.
The text consists of five phrases:
first, there is the person who commits the offense;
second, there is the circumstance of losing one's robe.

3. “A non-relative layperson, for the sake of one who has lost his robe, personally offers a robe and allows the bhikṣu to accept as much as he requires. This means that once the offering has been made three times, it is known to be sufficient.
Since one does not commit an offense with a relative, it is said that [the recipient] is "not a relative.
Fourth, regarding the phrase "this bhikṣu shall receive the robe with contentment," this means receiving it after measuring it.
Thus, the Vinaya states: "If one has lost even a single robe, one should not receive [another]."
If one loses two robes and only one remains—whether it be double, triple, or quadruple layered—one should tear it apart to fashion a saṃghāṭī and an uttarāsaṅga.
"If all three robes are lost, one should receive them with contentment.

The *Shu* says: "This means that if one robe is lost, receiving another is strictly not permitted; for with two robes remaining, it is sufficient for use while traveling between the two locations [the monastery and the lay community]."
If two robes are lost, according to the intent of the Vinaya texts, receiving [a new robe] is likewise not permitted.

If the remaining single robe has two layers, one may tear it to make two robes; however, since being short of one robe is equivalent in principle to having lost one, it is clear that receiving [a new robe] is not permitted.
If one possesses three layers of cloth and tears them apart to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), it is clearly not permissible to receive them.
Only when all three are lost may one be said to have received the three robes through the act of giving; this is because it maintains the integrity of faith and respect.
If one follows the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, it is permitted to receive only two [of the three robes] if all three are lost, with the remaining one to be sought elsewhere;
however, the intent of the present *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* differs from that.
5. Conclusion on the transgression and the resulting offense.
Eighth: The precept against, when a family intends to give, immediately encouraging them by voice to increase their expenditure so that they purchase fine robes.
Those of the old school call this "the precept against exhorting a single householder to increase the price of a robe"; its meaning is profound and subtle.
The text consists of four phrases:
first, the person who may commit the offense;
second, possessing the price and intending to purchase it to give to a bhikṣu.

3. "If this bhikṣu, without having first received the donor’s permission to seek more, then urges an increase," the Vinaya states: "If one increases it by even a single thread, or by even a sixteenth of a coin, one commits an offense."
4. The offense incurred by receiving the robe.
Ninth, the precept concerning the two families wishing to give.
The interpretation is the same as previously determined.
Tenth: The precept against pressuring a donor beyond the limit to solicit robes.
This text has two sections:
first, clarifying the offense of obtaining robes beyond the limit; second, clarifying the method for not exceeding the limit and thus not obtaining them.
The preceding text consists of three parts:
first, those who may be the offenders; second, the method of entrusting valuables and requesting clothing; third, the offense incurred by exceeding the time limit.
Within the second part, there are two sections: first, entrusting valuables; second, requesting clothing.
Regarding the entrustment of valuables, the textual analysis contains six sections:

first, the donor prepares the valuables; second, the messenger delivers them to the bhikṣu; third, the bhikṣu declines based on the teaching; fourth, he inquires about the location of the custodian; fifth, he sends the valuables to that person; and sixth, he returns to report to the bhikṣu.
Regarding the second section on "Requesting Robes," there are two parts:
first, an analysis of the three verbal requests; second, an explanation of the six silent requests.
Each of these two sections contains the formal procedures for requesting robes as well as the excellence of obtaining the robes.

Regarding the first three phrases, the text states: "A bhikṣu in need of robes should go to the place of the attendant and say, 'I require robes,' up until [the point where he specifies his needs]. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this is like a person entering a storehouse to take goods and placing them upon a shop counter for a moment, or like wrapping an object in a cloth bundle for a brief instant.
The phrase "If one obtains the robe after two or three requests, it is good" distinguishes the excellence of obtaining the robe, meaning it accords with the teaching.
Next, the text distinguishes the six instances of silence.

Regarding the statement, "If one does not obtain the robe, one should stand silently before [the donor] four times, five times, or six times," the text should actually proceed by accumulating from one or two times up to six times; however, the phrasing follows the momentum of the context to connect them directly.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "To remain silent means not speaking with the mouth; when invited to sit, one does not sit; when given food, one does not accept it; and one neither preaches the Dharma nor offers words of blessing."
If they ask,
"For what reason have you come here? answer:
"The householder knows for himself.
Furthermore, according to the Vinaya text: "If he says, 'I do not know,' and there is another person who does know, the bhikṣu should say to him:
'That person knows.'"

Furthermore, one instance of speech breaks two instances of silence; thus, if one seeks [the answer] using only speech, it may extend to six rounds, whereas if one seeks it using only silence, it may extend to twelve rounds.
The variations and alternations between these in the interim can be understood by reflection.
The remainder of the text is intelligible.
Next, the method for not exceeding or failing to obtain [the robe] is explained.
The meaning of the text states: "If it cannot be obtained, inform the original donor and have them return to reclaim it."
"This is the proper time" refers to the time when one does not lose faith in the giving of alms and acts in accordance with the Dharma.
Eleventh: The precept against begging for wild silkworm cotton to make bedding for oneself.
According to the origin story (*nidāna*) in the Vinaya, this was established because [the use of such items] caused injury to life and invited public censure.
Regarding the term "bedding" (*śayanāsana*), the tradition passed down from antiquity by Master Nanshan and others asserts that these are the three robes (*tricīvara*);
however, Tripiṭaka Master Jing states that they refer instead to items such as woolen rugs and mats.
Now, upon careful examination, this is precisely the "bed-covering robe" (wo-pi) used here in this region.
Therefore, the explanatory text for the precept concerning black wool bedding states: "If one makes a mattress or a felt rug, there is no offense."
Since it is called "bedding and requisites" (*śayanāsana*), we know it refers to a *pāṭa* (outer robe).

If one were to claim it refers to the three robes (*tricīvara*), then according to the rule that one commits an offense by making a new robe before six years have elapsed since discarding the old, how could it be that for the three robes one must necessarily discard the old before being permitted to make a new one?
Regarding the rule on the one-month robe (*māsa-cīvara*), if one continues to procure new materials, why would it be necessary to discard the old?

Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* refers to it as a "reclining implement" (*śayanāsana*), and the Vinaya-piṭaka masters of the Three Piṭakas likewise call it a "reclining implement. This may be because there are different categories, or because both upper and lower cloths are termed "reclining implements"; generally speaking, it refers to a shawl (*pāṭa*).
Furthermore, since a sleeping shawl (śayanapracchādana) is also suitable for being made into the three robes (tricīvara), there are instances of confusion in various teachings.
Moreover, because the sleeping shawl is an essential requisite, these various rules of regulation must exist.
This precept involves taking life; if one violates it and abandons [the training], the Vinaya mandates that they be executed and their body destroyed, which distinguishes it from other precepts.
Twelfth is the precept concerning bedding with black wool.
According to the Vinaya, this was established because of the conduct of those who were negligent.
Thirteenth: The precept concerning the addition of fine hair to bedding materials.
Formerly, this was called the "precept on white-hair bedding.

Examining the Vinaya text in detail now, it is clear that adding brindled hair does not constitute an offense, whereas adding any other types of hair constitutes an offense; thus, it is not restricted solely to white hair.
This means that even if one increases the black portion, one does not violate the preceding precept, because that preceding precept was established based solely on the middle portion.
The wording of the precept should state: "the second part is black, the third part is white, and the fourth part is variegated"; thus, the meaning is self-evident.
For example, regarding the four *kārṣāpaṇas* used for making bedding: two *kārṣāpaṇas* must be pure black, one *kārṣāpaṇa* white, and one *kārṣāpaṇa* variegated.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
Fourteenth: The precept against making a new bedding item within six years of its previous use.
This precept clarifies the formal acceptance and maintenance of bedding and requisites.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* and other texts, all garments that assist the body must be formally recognized and maintained. This is precisely why the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that apart from the three robes, if one stays overnight separated from any other garment, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If six years have passed and the robes are no longer fit for use, the formal undertaking (*dhāraṇa*) of the dharma is lost.
If they are less than six years old, one may relinquish the formal undertaking and make new ones again without offense.

If one wishes to travel far, or if one is ill or the robes are too heavy, the Saṃgha may grant permission through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion with one proclamation) to make new ones before the six years are up. One may then carry the new ones while traveling; as for the old ones, since the dharma has been relinquished, there is no offense in leaving them behind overnight.

When one returns from a journey and the illness has been cured, one should perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) for new items and continue to hold onto the old ones; this is the intended meaning.
If one performs the ritual of *śuddhi* on wealth to make bedding and so forth, why would there be a "six-year rule" regarding the eyes?
Why must one discard it?
Even if it is reduced by six years, it does not fall within the limit of an offense.
Fifteenth: The precept against using more than six sitting mats.
Regarding "one span" (*vitasti*), the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), fascicle 5, states: "It is the circumference of one span of the Sugata.
Regarding "discoloring" (*kasāya-varṇa*), it means to destroy the new color so as to cause one to be free from greedy attachment.
If, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one who lacks [the requisite] must seek it from another,
then according to this present *vinaya*, if one lacks it oneself, there is no offense provided one does not select [a specific object].

The sixteenth is the precept against carrying wool; the seventeenth is the precept against having a non-relative card wool; and the eighteenth is the precept against receiving precious objects. According to the explanation of the precept against possessing precious objects in the fifth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra*:

"If one merely takes hold of a precious object, it is subsumed under the ninety minor precepts (*navati-śaikṣa-dharma*); if one possesses a precious object, it is subsumed under the thirty precepts (*triṃśan-naiḥsargika-pāyattika*)."
That treatise states that there are five kinds of taking that constitute an offense:

first, taking by grasping with the hand; second, taking from another by means of clothing; third, taking from another by means of a vessel; fourth, saying, "Put it in this"; and fifth, saying, "Give this to the *śuddhika-puruṣa*. These are all offenses committed for the purpose of storing [the item].
Furthermore, according to that treatise, in the fourth fascicle concerning the precept on extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), one should seek two kinds of sponsors for purification (*viśuddhi-ādhāra*):
first, regarding money, precious objects, and the like, one should first seek a lay sponsor (*avadātavasana*) who knows the Dharma, instructing him with words intended for his understanding:
"I, a bhikṣu, am not permitted by the Dharma to possess money or precious objects."

"Now, you shall serve as the pure owner (*śuddhika*). When you later obtain money or precious goods, you must give them all away as a gift to the donor; this is the essential meaning of the formal request.
Later, when money or precious goods are obtained, one may declare them as pure (*śuddhi*) before the bhikṣu, without needing to state the name of the pure owner.
Once the purification (viśuddhi) has been declared, one may keep [the items] for as long or as short a time as desired.

Furthermore, according to that treatise, the section on the purification of money and treasures states there are two kinds; however, upon careful examination of the text, there are actually three kinds:
first, when a layperson brings money or treasures and gives them to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu simply says:
"This is an impure object; I should not keep it;
if it were pure, I would accept it.
Thus spoke the second bhikṣu.
"I should not keep it.
The attendant said,
"Keep it by exchanging it for pure items."
This constitutes the formal purification (*viśuddhi*); according to the treatise, this is subsumed within the preceding procedure.
Thirdly, if one simply leaves it on the ground, there must be a bhikṣu who performs the declaration of purity (*śuddhivācanā*); the logical phrasing for this is found in the initial passage.

Regarding the second point, the designator of purity (*śuddhikaraṇa-adhiṣṭhātṛ*): if a robe or robe-material exceeds the prescribed measure, one should seek out among the five groups of monks a person who maintains the precepts, is learned, and possesses virtue to serve as the designator of purity.
If one possesses a robe of proper measure that has not been purified (*pariṣkāra*), one commits an offense of forfeiture and expiation (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If one possesses a robe of improper measure that has not been purified, one commits an offense of forfeiture; one must perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is explained in detail in that treatise. That treatise further states: "There are five kinds of things that should be purified (*pariṣkāra*):

first, precious gems; second, coins and objects resembling jewels; third, clothing and clothed goods exceeding the prescribed measurement; fourth, all clothing and clothed goods not exceeding the prescribed measurement; and fifth, all grains and rice."
Grain, rice, and so forth must be purified on that very day.
If no layperson is available, they may be purified in the presence of the fourfold assembly.
If one does not purify them, one commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense at the conclusion of the day; one must confess a *duṣkṛta*.
In this present precept, the intention is to distinguish precious objects and money; all other matters are distinguished by association with these.
Furthermore, according to the Vinaya, once this precept and the subsequent one have been violated, one should relinquish the object to a pure person (śuddhika-pudgala) and say:
"This object is not for me to possess; you should know this."
According to this, it constitutes the formula for *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (the declaration of purity).
Therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Once the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* has been performed, one may then enter the assembly to confess [one's transgressions]."
Furthermore, former teachers stated that the two types of precious objects—those kept as property or those traded—are subject exclusively to the *pārivāsika-saṃghāvaśeṣa* confession.

Now, examining the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*, since it states that one enters the assembly, we know that this confession also applies generally to the *saṃgha*; once the confession is completed, [the offense is cleared].
If he returns pure items such as robes or alms bowls in exchange, this is in accordance with the Dharma.

If they are sent directly, one should accept them while maintaining the thought that they belong to a "pure master," and employ the formal words for acknowledging purity (*jñapti-vāda*), thereby instructing a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible) to know how to trade for pure items and receive and maintain them.
If one does not say, "I see it" or "I know it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
this should be understood according to the Vinaya.
If that person does not return [the item], and one employs skillful means to seek it back, this is also adjudicated according to the Vinaya.
Furthermore, regarding confession before others, the relinquishment of material goods is as previously described.

Next, concerning the confession of offenses: there are the *śiṣṭāpatti* (offenses involving forfeiture) for the use of such goods, the *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses), the *mṛṣāvāda* (false speech), and the root *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses). Each of these has six grades of concealment (*chādana*) and subsequent concealment (*anvachādana*), which, when combined with the *duṣkṛta* of using [the goods] and the *mṛṣāvāda*, total eight grades of *duṣkṛta* and so forth; these should be confessed according to the procedure for the *atirekacīvara* (excess robe) offense described above.
Nineteenth is the precept against trading in precious objects.
This refers to the successive exchange of precious items; it constitutes an offense against all seven classes of followers. Whether committed by oneself or incited in others, both are offenses.
The expression "buying and selling" is simply another term for mutual trade.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika*, if one trades with an object after it has been purified (*viśuddha*), it constitutes an offense.
The procedure for relinquishing and repenting this offense is the same as for the preceding precepts; one should know this. The twentieth is the precept against buying and selling.

This refers to engaging in trade with laypeople—whether at appropriate or inappropriate times, for a period of seven days or for life—including new clothing and other goods, by haggling over prices according to the methods of the marketplace.
If one trades with the five groups of the ordained, there is no offense;
this should be understood according to the Vinaya.
Twenty-first: The precept against keeping an extra alms bowl.

This is explained according to the section on extra robes (*atirekacīvara*): that is to say, if a donor offers it of their own volition or one acquires it by purchasing it oneself, one commits this precept;
if one begs it from another, one commits the subsequent precept.
The twenty-second precept concerns begging for a bowl.

This means that if one already possesses a bowl broken into five pieces that is still fit for repair and use, yet one further begs for another, the offense of forfeiture is incurred as soon as it is obtained.
In the text, from the passage "That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it" onwards, the methods for relinquishing and repenting are analyzed.
For all precepts, there are four stages:
first, the relinquishment of the object; second, the repentance of the offense; third, the restoration of the dharma; and fourth, the incurrence of the offense if it is not restored.
Now, this one precept differs from the others in that it involves two methods for relinquishing it—returning the object and formally renouncing the rule—and is therefore recited separately.

The text states, "That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and relinquish [it]"; this is the first recitation, the formula for relinquishment. This differs from other precepts, which may be relinquished before one, two, or three individuals, or before the Saṃgha, or within a great boundary (mahā-sīmā), a boundary of the precept-platform (sīmā-maṇḍala), or a natural boundary (prakṛti-sīmā), as appropriate.
Now, this begging of the bowl is restricted to its relinquishment before the Saṃgha within the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) of this specific residence.
At the time of relinquishing it, one should perform the proper ritual and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

I, Bhikṣu [Name], have a bowl that is broken with fewer than five mends and is not leaking; yet I have further begged for a new bowl, numbering two, three, or more as the case may be, thereby committing an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya of the first, second, or third degree.
"Now, I relinquish this to the Sangha; [this is] declared once.

Next, regarding the confession (*pratideśanā*), one should understand by analogy that there are also eight categories of *dukkaṭa* offenses, such as those involving the use of a bowl for which a forfeiture has been incurred.
The fourth [category], the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), is easy to explain and requires no further elaboration.
However, I shall now explain the third [category] to clarify the method of returning.

The precept text states: "Passing it along, one should take the lowest bowl and give it to him to hold; he should continue to hold it even until it is broken—this is the proper time, meaning the time when it accords with the Dharma."
According to the Vinaya, one should retain a fine bowl and return the lowest-quality one.

If, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one obtains a very expensive bowl through begging, it should be sold; ten portions of the proceeds should be taken, with nine portions entering the Sangha and one portion returned to the owner.
In this Vinaya, one should simply take back the lower bowl and need not follow that [other practice].
Regarding the ritual for returning it, according to the Vinaya there are four sections:
first, the determination of its quality, as explained above.
2. Second, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion with one announcement) for permission to exchange back. 3.

Still fearing that [the other bowl] might be superior, one must again perform the *ekajñapti-karman* (single announcement) within the Saṃgha to exchange it; one should exchange it for the lowest-ranking bowl and return it. At the time of exchange, it is left to the discretion of the Saṃgha: whether one returns it immediately or exchanges it on the spot, if other monks wish to exchange, they may do so as they please; if they do not wish to exchange, they likewise follow the will of the Saṃgha. This should be understood according to the Vinaya.
4. Only after performing the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) may it be returned to its original owner.
What the ancients called "punishing [the offender] by making him use the old while holding the new" refers to this.

Regarding the phrase in the *karman* text, "to grant and cause to hold," this does not mean that the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is added for the purpose of formal possession; rather, it simply means to receive and then practice it.

Therefore, the fifth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "The bowl previously received and maintained was received and maintained in accordance with the Dharma; as for the subsequent bowl, it was not formally received, yet one was simply required to keep it constantly."
"At mealtime, one should carry two bowls; this should be done thus for the rest of one's life to demonstrate the fault of excessive greed.
Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The old bowl must be disassembled and mended every day; even if it is finished in a single day, it must be thoroughly washed."

If one knows that the teacher-monks are mindful of this virtuous bhikṣu and fear that he might hinder their meditation and recitation, and thus they break it or hide it away, there is no offense in using a new one.

Therefore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "One should even break [the old one] and take [the new one]," yet it further requires that one protect and maintain it rather than discarding it or damaging it at will; this should be understood according to the Vinaya.
Twenty-third: The precept against begging for thread from a non-relative and having a non-relative weave it into a robe.

To examine the intent of this precept: first, because many such conditions obstruct the Path; second, because they invite public censure; and third, because they cause harm to others and thereby accumulate transgressions.

To request thread for the purpose of manufacturing [robes] involves many conditions; to request it from one who is not a relative incurs censure. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, to use one's influence to compel a weaver to weave without providing payment constitutes harming others.

If any one of these three factors is lacking, there is no offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), just as, for example, there is no offense of exceeding the prescribed dimensions when building a hut by begging for materials oneself.
Twenty-fourth: The precept against knowing that another intends to give a gift and secretly encouraging them to have it woven well.
Twenty-fifth: The precept against taking back a robe after having requested it as a gift, which was not granted.
Guangyuan states: "The original giving of the robe was not shared; this clarifies that it constitutes a case of forceful seizure."
The former interpretation—that one merely names someone else as the recipient of the robe and later seizes it in violation of the precepts—is altogether too obscure.
According to the Vinaya texts, having first given the robe to another while inwardly harboring a desire to reclaim it, one personally intends to go among the people to teach and transform them;
because the other person does not leave afterward, one seizes the robe back out of anger.
This constitutes the offense of taking back what was given indifferently after having taken it with certainty.
If one takes back what was given with certainty and taken with certainty, or what was given with certainty and taken indifferently—these two cases of taking back constitute a grave offense.
If both are indeterminate, taking [the medicine] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The twenty-sixth precept concerns the storage of medicine for more than seven days.
The text consists of five phrases:
I. The person who may commit the offense;
II. The circumstances for a sick person to store medicine;
III. Regarding "residual medicine," the phrase "ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar" enumerates the five types of medicinal substances.
According to the Vinaya, bear fat and similar substances, when strained clear like oil, are subsumed under the category of "oil.
Fourth, regarding the phrase "one may take [medicine] for seven days," this refers to the addition of a formal oral authorization that sets a time limit for its consumption.
5. From "If [the time] has passed" onwards, the offense is concluded.
Upon reaching the eighth day at the appearance of dawn (*aruṇodgama*), one commits the offense immediately without waiting for ingestion;
furthermore, at the time of ingestion, one commits additional offenses such as consuming impure medicine or that which has been defiled by residue.
Because it is not clearly understood in the text, it is referred to as "a dose.

As for the term "residual medicine" (*śeṣa-bhaiṣajya*) mentioned in the text: just as the *dhāraṇī-cīvara* (extra robe) is defined in contrast to the three robes (*tricīvara*), here "residual medicine" refers to that which remains after one dose, intended for several more doses, and is thus termed "residual."
If one receives [the medicine] by mouth, it is without fault even if consumed after seven days have passed; however, once the seven days have elapsed, consuming it constitutes a transgression.

Based on this, the meanings of "timely" (*kāla*) and "untimely" (*akāla*), "seven-day" (*saptāha*), "lifelong" (*yāvajjīva*), and the "four medicines" (*catvāri bhaiṣajyāni*) are collectively explained through two sections:
first, defining the names and determining their essential nature; second, the method of receiving and maintaining them.

First, to explain the names and define their essential nature: regarding what is called "timely medicine" (*kālabhaiṣajya*), it is restricted to the period before noon. Because it serves to treat the primary illness, sustain the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and alleviate hunger while nourishing the karmic retribution, it is termed "timely."
"Proper time" (*kāla*) and "improper time" (*akāla*): the meaning of the Sūtra is based on this principle.

Regarding "improper time," grape juice and similar drinks—which cure thirst, alleviate cold, and treat both primary and secondary ailments—are called "improper time" when they are permitted to be drunk after midday until the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodaya*).

Regarding the "seven-day" period: for illnesses such as those caused by wind or phlegm where the pathogenic forces are somewhat strong, the medicinal efficacy only manifests after seven days of continuous treatment; thus it is called "seven days.

As for chronic conditions such as abdominal tumors (*pi*), nodules (*zheng*), or kidney accumulations (*shenji*), which are only gradually diminished over time, long-term administration is permitted; this is termed "throughout one's life" (*jin-xing*).

However, while the matters regarding the other three medicines are easy to understand, people often take the medicine for life indiscriminately; therefore, in determining the essential nature of this medicine, four conditions must be met:

first, the body must have a condition that can be treated, such as hunger or thirst, which are considered ordinary "primary illnesses. Thus, the Vinaya states that taking a medicine for life when there is no cause or condition for illness constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Paramārtha says:
"To consume ghee and the like without being ill is to commit the offense of eating at an improper time (*vikālabhojana*)."

Second, regarding what is required for medical prescriptions: even in medicinal formulas, it is permitted to include a portion of food that must be eaten at the proper time, let alone other ingredients.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "A bhikṣu who lives on alms saw someone making stone honey (śarkarā-madhu) mixed with woolen cloth (karpāsa); having doubts about it, he did not eat it."
The Buddha said:
"The ritual procedure should be performed in this manner.

Furthermore, as stated in the sixth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*: "Whether using a medicinal substance of the 'timely' category (*kālabhaiṣajya*) or one of the 'seven-day' category (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), it may be transformed into a 'lifetime' medicine (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*); there is no fault in taking it."

Third, there are those whose nature as medicine is universally recognized by the world, such as *fuling* (poria cocos) and dried *dihuang* (remanopanax pseudosinensis); there is no one in the world who does not know that their substance is medicinal, and they are required in the majority of all prescriptions.
If one does not permit their consumption, it would deeply contradict the intention of the Sage. The Vinaya Master of Nanshan said:

"Now there are foolish people who, at improper times, forgetfully consume powdered dried turmeric, *fuling* (poria cocos), and so forth. These are not only salty and bitter enough to choke the mouth, but they are also taken out of mere whim; they are no better than eating plain rice."
Now, upon careful examination, this is a profoundly erroneous judgment.

For instance, regarding the origin story (*nidāna*) of the seven-day medicine, it says: "There are five kinds of medicine known to the world; they should be eaten as food or used as medicine, and must not appear coarse."
"If even coarse food was permitted by the Buddha for consumption, why would he not allow pine fungus (fuling) as medicine?
Fourth, regarding the departure from the practice of eating at the proper time:
according to this, [the rule] does not require one to appear coarse for seven days; how much less so now that it concerns the remainder of one's life—how could it be otherwise?"

I have heard of those who, after midday has passed, prepare flour for evening porridge and use thick tea as a substitute for eye-salve, further using ginger and vinegar as a cold rinse; this is truly not as good as eating rice.
This constitutes the very basis for indulging in greed and delusion; it is not a vessel for the path of cultivation, and therefore it must certainly be abandoned.

Furthermore, that which is universally known in the world to be medicinal—if it enters into a medicinal compound, it is clearly permitted; even if one wishes to take it alone, there is no fault in doing so.

However, among those who are ill, if there should be someone who has gone entirely without food for a full day, and who fears that excessive hunger and thirst may give rise to a secondary ailment, they are permitted to take medicine.
By this principle, there is no aspect of the matter left unaddressed.
Next, regarding the method for receiving and maintaining [the medicines], ancient authorities cite the question posed by Upāli in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:

"How does one avoid transgressing with respect to the *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the current time), the *saptāha-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for seven days), and the *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for life)?"
"Is it permissible to receive [food] by hand or by word when it has been kept overnight or seized improperly?
The Buddha said, "It is permissible."

Furthermore, the sixth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If a sick bhikṣu requires medicine for seven days, and it is difficult to obtain because he has no attendant (kappiya-kāraka) to request it on his behalf, he should receive it directly from the hands of one who is pure."
"Having received [the medicine] from the mouth of a bhikṣu, place it in one spot and take it yourself to eat within seven days.
This is precisely why the present *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "It may be consumed for up to seven days."
First, we shall distinguish the *vikāla-pāna* (unseasonable drinks), analyzing them according to three points:
first, the medicine received; second, the person who bestows it; and third, the actual application of the ritual formula (*vidhi*). Regarding the first point:

for the most part, they are made from fruits, though some are prepared from roots; or else various syrups are fermented using medicinal substances and the like, such as the eight kinds of syrups mentioned in the *Bhaiṣajya-vastu*.
The seventeenth commentary of the *Samantapāsādikā* states: "All fruit from trees may be made into non-time juice (*vikāla-pāna*), with the exception of various grains.
All leaves may be made into non-time juice; vegetables such as potherbs and tea leaves are precisely what constitute non-time juice."
All flowers may be worn as non-seasonal attire, with the exception of the *mātuluṅga* flower and the lotus flower, etc.
Among all fruits, those of the *tāla* tree, the coconut, the gourd, and the like are excluded.
The details are as found in that treatise.
As for fermented liquors, such as *suvīra* gruel, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi) volume 29 states: "Fermented from parched barley."
This Vinaya refers to the medical instruction to consume fermented barley juice.

These various types of fermented liquids must be free from eight defects: namely, impure contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*), self-cooking, cooking inside [the vessel], being left overnight, being stored overnight, change of substance (meaning the loss of its original flavor), not having been received with the hands, and having been placed on the ground after receiving it and left for more than a brief moment—meaning past the "non-time" (*akāla*) of a brief moment; according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this constitutes a loss of the formal reception (*pratigraha*).

Second, the person who bestows [the drink] must know the method for preparing the gruel. For example, when making grape juice, the grapes must be purified by fire; once pressed into juice, it must be purified by dripping water over it. If either is impure, or both are impure, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 26, it is not permitted to drink it.

If the liquid is turbid and not yet clear, and the attendant (kappiya-kāraka) wishes to leave, one may boil it once so that it can be reheated later; this does not constitute the offense of boiling for oneself. However, if it is intended for raw drinking, boiling is not required.
When the *karmadāna* (lay attendant) hands it over, he should form the intention of giving it to the bhikṣu.
When the bhikṣu receives it, he should clearly recognize the previous drink, hold out his hand, and receive it by suspending it in mid-air.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, he should address the bhikṣu as follows:

"In this regard, when pure substances arise, one should think, 'I shall accept these,' and this is the method of formal identification (*saṃjñā-dharma*), meaning that one must wait for them to become clear and then accept them in accordance with the Dharma.
Once they have become clear, it is sufficient merely to accept them; no further formal identification is required."

Regarding the third [method], the formal addition (*pratikṣepa*): in various schools, there are only instructions for adding the formula but no specific textual wording; it should be recited according to the meaning.
Having performed the proper ritual, one should face a single bhikṣu, hold the medicine in hand, and say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!..."
I, bhikṣu [name], now for the purpose of treating thirst, have this grape juice; desiring to consume it from the beginning of the night, I now receive it from the Venerable One—thus three times.
"If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food), one may receive it with the hand at any time and drink it repeatedly; this method [of formal acceptance] is not required.
One should know that for all other types of fermented drinks (*pāna*), the name is changed accordingly.
Although the newly translated *Vinaya-saṃgraha* contains textual passages regarding the addition of these methods, we shall follow the ancient tradition for now.
Next, the seven-day medicines also have three categories:
as for the substance of the medicine, it refers to the five types mentioned in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*;
furthermore, they are free from the eight defects. Regarding the specific distinctions among them, there are three types of "leftover overnight" [medicines]:
The first point is as previously stated.
Second, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, this does not refer to medicines for other bhikṣus that have exceeded the seven-day limit.
Third, it does not refer to medicines that one has already violated by oneself, nor to those that have already reached the seventh day or beyond.
The remaining seven items are the same as above.
Regarding the second point, the person who bestows [the medicine] must cook and strain it according to the Dharma, distinguishing it from "timely food" (*kālabhojana*).
Should they not be distinguished, the identification is as before: for example, fat is [distinguished by] having its dregs removed; the same applies to oil and other such substances.

Receiving [the medicine] with the hands is governed by the same rules as before. If one forms the intention to consume it, or if one intends to apply it to the feet and so forth, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is not accomplished.
Third, regarding the actual application of the rite: first, one must ensure that one has not previously kept the medicine in excess, thereby committing the offense of *atireka*.
If one has previously committed an offense of excess and now receives [the precepts] again, one is immediately stained by the offense.
The ritual manual states:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!..."

I, Bhikṣu [Name], now for the purpose of treating a wind-related illness, accept from the Venerable One this sesame oil—a seven-day medicine—intended to be consumed for seven nights; this I do, having stated it three times.
The Vinaya Master of the Southern Mountain, following the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-uttaragrantha*, prescribed taking the seven-day medicines within the purified area (*śuddhasthāna*).

Now, upon examining that treatise, it is clear that the latter three types of medicine are all prohibited from being kept overnight; however, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* permits keeping the lifelong medicines overnight. Therefore, one should know that [the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-uttaragrantha*] is not the same as that [Vinaya].
Other illnesses and other medicines should be understood according to the preceding rules.
Next, the medicines for as long as life lasts (*yāvajjīvikauṣadha*) are distinguished; they are free from the eight defects mentioned above regarding fermented liquids (*mantha*).

Second, regarding the person who may administer them: the Master of Vinaya of the Southern Mountains (*Nanshan lishi*), following the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), permits that cold food may be boiled again.
If [the grain] has sprouted, it is permitted to cook it after performing the purification by fire.
Now, examining the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this provision for cooking after purification applies specifically to sprouting seeds.
If one considers other types such as rice or flour that are not sprouting seeds, would there not be permission to cook them oneself?

Therefore, one should know that if the characteristic of "cooked" (pakva) arises through mere transformation, one commits the offense of cooking for oneself; thus, one must wait until the transformation has occurred before it is no longer an offense to cook.
Regarding the marking of the food, receiving it with the hand, and so forth, these should be understood according to the preceding rules.
Regarding the third method, the addition of the correct [mantra], both the general and specific applications are effective.
As for the specific reception, it is like the four equal pills (*catuḥsama-guṭikā*).
If one first obtains ginseng (*renshen*), one should say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], because of the condition of weak mental and physical strength, shall partake of these four kinds of medicinal substances for as long as my life lasts. Desiring to keep them overnight and consume them regularly, I now receive them from you, Venerable sir, through this twofold declaration."
"The remaining parts should be understood accordingly.
If one is to receive them all together, one should say in total:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!"

I, Bhikṣu [Name], because of the cause and condition of having little strength of mind due to illness, take these four medicinal pills—which are medicines for life—to be kept with me overnight; the remaining wording is as above.

When going to the market to purchase medicine, once the *karmadāna* (attendant) has settled the price, the bhikṣu may select for himself an excessive amount. Afterward, he should have it weighed and receive it in successive portions, ensuring that it is not placed on the ground. He must then immediately seek out another bhikṣu to perform the ritual of formal acceptance (*adhivāsanā*); this is then in accordance with the Dharma.
Because he previously took much [of the goods] while they were not yet definitively assigned to him, he did not commit the offense of improper contact (*duṣṭasparśa*).
Since he accepted them only after they had been formally designated as his, it constitutes purity.
Although the various Dharma masters speak loftily of the methods for severing delusions on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), though their talk may be grand, it has no bearing upon themselves.

Now, regarding this Vinaya, which governs the gates of one’s own practice and requires the mind to be restrained in accordance with the teachings—if in every matter one acts contrary to them, how can such a person be called one who possesses knowledge and understanding?
To break the *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses) is not to cross the great ocean; why then do you refuse to believe, recklessly indulging in greed and delusion?
Alas, alas! How deeply lamentable this is!

Those who uphold these teachings mostly correctly prevent the faults of losing what has been received and thus not having received it at all, as well as the faults of keeping food overnight, improper contact, cooking within, and storing within.

If one expects [the medicine] to be cooked by oneself and so forth, although it does not constitute formal acceptance (*pratigraha*), there is no violation of the dharma regarding the prevention of wrongdoing through verbal expression.

The old [commentary] states that for the seven-day [medicine], internal cooking is not prohibited during the improper time; however, since the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* simply states that internal cooking is permitted for life-long [medicine], I have now examined and determined that it is consistent with the prohibition [of internal cooking] for life-long medicine, without error.
The twenty-seventh: the precept concerning the use of a rain-bathing robe before the previous period has expired.
These two precepts were established together.
Regarding the phrase "one month remaining of spring": from the middle of the first month to the middle of the fourth month, a total of three months constitutes the spring season.
When one month remains of the middle of spring, it refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the third month onwards.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "On the sixteenth day of the third month, one should seek the rain-bath robe."

Regarding the phrase "one should bathe during the half-month," this means that from the sixteenth day of the third month onward, when the count reaches the full half-month, it is the first day of the fourth month; therefore, the Vinaya states, "on the first day of the fourth month, one should bathe."
The remaining text is easy to understand.
Regarding the dimensions of the rain-bathing robe, they are as described in the ninety precepts below.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, fascicle six, states: "First, when it rains from heaven, one uses [the robe] to shield the four sides while bathing therein."
First, when it is hot during the summer, they also use it as a screen to bathe within its shade.
Second, because there is much rain in the summer, they wrap their three robes in it to carry them while traveling back and forth.
The twenty-eighth: The precept concerning receiving an urgent offering of robes before the [end of the] period, or keeping them after the [period has passed].
These two precepts are also established together.

Regarding the text stating, "Ten days remaining before the end of the three-month summer retreat," this means that after eighty days have passed during the preceding *anvārohaṇa* (rainy-season retreat), ten days still remain before the ninety-day period is completed.
This shall be from the sixth to the fifteenth day of the seventh month, totaling ten days; during these ten days, it is permitted to receive and accept an urgent gift on whichever day one obtains it.
The Buddha has established a rule that once the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is concluded, one is not permitted to receive robes; to receive them before then constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

However, in cases where a donor has urgent business requiring travel to a distant location and cannot wait until the end of the summer, it is permitted to offer the gift within the ten days preceding the conclusion of the retreat. This is known as the "robe of urgent necessity" (*ātyayika-cīvara*).

Regarding the phrase "having received [the robe], one should keep it until the time for robes": after the summer retreat has ended, the month of Kārttika or the five months [following] are both termed the "time for robes."
During the period for wearing robes, it is not necessary to perform the ritual of "purification" (śuddhi); one may simply keep them.
This refers to those who received [the robes] on the sixth day of the seventh month; they may keep them for one full month after the summer retreat has ended, totaling five months.
If one receives [the precepts] on the seventh day of the seventh month, one may keep them for an additional day after the first and fifth months.
If one receives them on the eighth day of the seventh month, one may keep them for an additional two days thereafter.
Even for those who receive [the robes] on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, they may keep them for an additional nine days thereafter.
Any violation based on exceeding this limit constitutes an offense, as explained in detail in the Vinaya.

Twenty-ninth: The precept concerning the permission to be separated from the three robes for up to six nights during the month of Kārttika while staying in an araṇya (forest hermitage) when there is doubt or fear.

Regarding the statement, "When the month of Kārttika is full," according to the other three Vinayas, this refers to those who have completed the later retreat (*paścimaka-varṣā*). Since they have not yet been permitted to depart during the month of Kārttika, and those who completed the earlier retreat (*pūrvaka-varṣā*) have already all departed, there is a fear that those remaining alone may encounter dangers from external bandits. Therefore, it is permitted to send whichever of the three robes (*tricīvara*) is most excellent to a dwelling in a village to be kept for six nights. By the time of the dawn of the sixth night, one must assemble the robes together and stay overnight; thereafter, one may again keep them deposited for another six nights.
The claim by former masters that one may receive a "consigned robe" (*nikṣipta-cīvara*) after the completion of the *kārttika* month is erroneous.
