The thirtieth [offense], the precept against diverting property belonging to the Saṃgha for one's own use:

according to the origin story (*nidāna*) in the Vinaya, if one knows that a donor intends to give property to the *saṃmukhībhūta-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha present before one) but their mind is not yet fixed, and one diverts it to seek inclusion for oneself, one commits this offense.

If one diverts property belonging to the Sangha of the four directions to enter one's own immediate presence, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense according to the Vinaya, because the property has not been incorporated into one's own possession;
however, if it were incorporated into one's own possession, one would likewise incur an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If one knows that the intention is definitely to give to the Sangha, yet it is certainly diverted to oneself, then according to principle, this constitutes a grave offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 11, states: "If someone brings an object to offer, the bhikṣu should instruct them to give it to the Sangha, as this will yield great karmic fruit."
"If one says, 'I have already given this to the Sangha,' there is no offense in receiving it.
The third section concludes with a summary for careful retention; it is easy to understand as written.
Regarding the confession and relinquishment of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, the text omits details because they may vary according to the specific precepts.
From here begins the fifth major section: the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas of individual offenses.
The textual structure has three parts as before.

Within the second part, the enumeration of the names and characteristics of the offenses, the first is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). Having committed this offense, one receives retribution in hell for twenty-one billion and forty thousand years by human reckoning.
Should one be reborn later, whatever they seek will be empty and without fruit.
These are subsumed under the ten non-virtues, and the karmic paths involved are particularly profound.
If many people are not careful, they will wander through the evil realms, with no known time for liberation.
Second, disparaging speech by way of class refers to reviling a bhikṣu by comparing him to an extremely lowly class, such as saying, "You resemble a butcher," and so forth.

Fourth, regarding sleeping in the same room with a woman: regardless of whether she is a monastic or a layperson, or whether she is a relative or a stranger, the object of the act is taken to be one who possesses intelligence and whose life-force is not severed; therefore, it is known that this refers to a "great woman."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, fascicle eight, states: "If one is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse—such as with a barren woman, or even a female pigeon—it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one touches a human woman as she turns or rolls onto her side, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each instance."
However, according to the Vinaya texts, there are four characteristics of a room:
first, having enclosures on all four sides with a roof above—meaning it is completely enclosed and completely covered;
second, being screened at the front but lacking walls—meaning it is completely covered but has many enclosures, which refers to having enclosures on three sides.
Third, although it is covered, it is not all-encompassing; this refers to cases where all obstructions are half-covered.
Fourth, although it is covered, there are openings; this refers to cases where all obstructions are mostly covered.
An ancient Vinaya text adds a further phrase, "there are four walls with no covering above," but this is an error.
The nine types [of dwellings] that do not constitute a *śālā* (room) are analogous to this fourth *śālā*.
The nine types of *śālā* will be explained later.
Within these four types of *śālā*, one commits an offense whenever one turns over or shifts position.

Furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, within a single roof and a single enclosure there may be several small rooms; although the rooms are distinct from one another, because the hall is the same, it constitutes a single offense of *thullaccaya* (a grave offense).

Furthermore, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when preaching the Dharma throughout the night during a great assembly, if there is wind, rain, cold, or snow covering the ground, one should enter an inner room and sit with the body upright.
If one is too old or ill to sit, one should provide a screen or partition; however, one must not use coarse or thin materials.
The height should reach from the shoulders and armpits down to the ground, so that not even a kitten can pass through.
When traveling on the road or entering a village, one should stay in a separate room; if no room is available, one should follow the aforementioned method.
An ancient commentary states:
When sitting with the body upright, there must be lamp-light and several people present.

If a partition is set up, one must draw a continuous line from the wall within the room, extending through the center of the doorway out to the front of the dwelling, forming the appearance of two rooms; only then is it not an offense.
Furthermore, upon examining the ancients, they followed the Vinaya by combining three sets of three to form nine types of non-completion of the characteristics of a dwelling (*anāvasatha*).
Now, upon detailed inspection, there are only eight phrases that constitute the characteristics of a non-dwelling; the inclusion of nine phrases is an error in the Vinaya text.
Furthermore, the enumeration of the nine cases consists of three sets of three. Regarding the first set of three:

first, being entirely covered with no obstruction at all; second, being entirely covered with half an obstruction; and third, being entirely covered with a small obstruction, meaning there is a wall on one side.

Regarding the second set of three: first, "exhausting the obstacles of the non-obscuring" (the phrase "further adding one sentence erroneously" mentioned previously refers to this); second, "exhausting the obstacles of the semi-obscuring"—this phrase exists in the original Vinaya text, whereas its absence here is an error.

This phrase establishes the chamber; it now falls within this "non-establishment" because it is identical to the third chamber among the four chambers previously established. Having exhausted the three [obstructions] and noting that there is little covering here, the explanation of the second triad is concluded.
Regarding the third set of three: first, half-covered and half-obstructed; second, slightly covered and slightly obstructed; third, neither covered nor obstructed.
Among these nine phrases, with the exception of the second phrase within the second set of three, one commits no offense when walking or sitting upon the remaining eight phrases.
However, the Vinaya does not state that one commits no offense while lying down; if one lies down due to illness, there is no offense whatsoever.
All subsequent descriptions of room characteristics should be understood according to this principle.
Fifth: The precept against staying overnight for more than three nights in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination.
According to the Vinaya, if one does not avoid the appearance of light during the third night, it constitutes one *pāyattika* offense.
Nanshan states that this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; however, this contradicts the wording of the precept, which states that three nights constitute a *pāyattika*.
Upon reaching the fourth night, one should acknowledge each offense committed while lying on one's side.

If one avoided the appearance of light during the third night and thus fully separated from it by one full night upon reaching the fourth, yet if one did not separate from it, one still commits an offense for lying on one's side; the rules regarding the room are the same as before.
I lack the leisure to discuss in detail the similarities and differences regarding other disciplinary rules.
Sixth, reciting the precepts together with those who have not yet received the precepts;
this refers to chanting the Buddha’s Tripiṭaka teachings in unison.
According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, if one composes a written record oneself and recites it together with others, there is no offense.
According to the Vinaya, when teaching a disciple the scriptures, one should say:
"When I have finished speaking, you shall speak."
If one does not act thus, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
According to the sixth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, if two people both have received the transmission of the text and recite it together, there is no offense.
Based on this, if each person performs their own primary task and there is no intention to harmonize the voices, there is no offense.
When the chant leader on the platform recites "All [recite together]," each person should recite for themselves; this is the standard procedure for opening the service.
According to the *Mātṛkā*, if two people chant in unison, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; the sixth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states the same.
Seventh, the precept against disclosing another’s grave offense to one who is not fully ordained.

Regarding the phrase "except by formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-karman*)," according to the Vinaya, when Devadatta was about to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, the Buddha ordered Śāriputra to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint him to publicly announce Devadatta’s faults among the assembly of laypeople; therefore, [the monk] did not commit an offense.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), fascicle 6, states: "It would be better to destroy a stupa or damage an image than to speak of the faults of a bhikṣu to one who has not yet received full ordination; if one speaks of them, one destroys the Dharma-body."
Eighth: To preach the precepts to one who has not yet received full ordination while claiming to have personally realized the Path.
This is not an offense committed by ordinary or inferior persons, and therefore it is not explained in detail.
Ninth: To preach the Dharma to a woman with more than five or six words when no man of intelligence is present.
The phrase "five or six words" refers to five or six categories.
For example, the five aggregates constitute five categories, and the six sense bases constitute six categories; explaining these five or six categories in detail does not constitute an offense.
If there is a wise man nearby acting as a third person to distinguish between the defiled and the pure, there is no limit to his number.
According to the sixth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, he must necessarily be a layman; a monastic may not serve this purpose, even though their status is similar.

If one follows this Vinaya, the subsequent text states that when a jewel is held by a husband, a fourth person is permitted; when not held by a husband, a third person is permitted; and when sitting in the open with a woman, a third person is permitted.
The Vinaya texts both state: "If there are two bhikṣus acting as companions, there is no offense.
This standard is thus different from that of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun).
Tenth: The precept against digging the earth.
This refers to ground that is moist and capable of producing grasses and trees.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, destroying such ground—even to the extent of a mosquito’s leg—constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.
If it is necessary to dig, one should employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) and say:
"To look at it is to know it.
If one were simply told, "Dig this," one commits a *thullaccaya* offense.
Eleventh, the precept against destroying living seeds.
The Vinaya states that "ghosts and spirits" are not human beings.

Now, upon careful examination, "non-humans" (amanusya) generally encompass the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*); thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle ten, says: "That is to say, they are born from plants and trees, and sentient beings dwell depending upon them."
"Sentient beings" refers to tree spirits and so forth, down to mosquitoes, gadflies, scorpions, insects, and ants.
Examining the general purport of the Vinaya, there are two kinds of birth:
first, those from roots, branches, and the like; second, those from grains, wheat, and the like.
For each individual type of grain and for each individual grain that is broken, there is one *pāyattika* offense.
If one eats fruits, vegetables, or the like along with their seeds, one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") perform the purification by fire (*aggi-parisodhana*) upon pure ground.
If one does not eat the seeds, one may break them with a knife, remove the kernels with the nails and fingers, and then eat them.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 14, if a *karmadāna* knows that there is unrefined grain in the storehouse and fears that young bhikṣus do not understand the Dharma, he may have a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) purify it by fire; from that point until the grain is completely exhausted, they may constantly speak of it as "pounded" and there is no offense.
The details are as found in the various Vinayas.
Twelfth, regarding the phrase "falsely making divergent speech to annoy others": to "falsely" means to falsely rely upon or invoke another matter.
As in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, volume fourteen, it asks:
"From where have you come? and he replies: [as follows].
Where does it come from in the past?
Where does it go? Answer:
"To go away in a future life"—
one who answers incorrectly in this manner is said to be "speaking otherwise.
According to the Vinaya, when Chanda treats others with contempt and utters such speech of speaking otherwise, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When a Buddhist bhikṣu performs the *jñapti-dharma* (the formal motion) and speaks otherwise than what was agreed upon, it is called "speaking differently.
If he commits a further offense after the motion has been made, he incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave) offense.

On subsequent days, Chanda again disturbed the Saṃgha; when summoned by the Saṃgha he would not come, yet came when not summoned; he would remain silent when he ought to speak, and spoke when he ought not to speak.
To act in this irrational manner is called "causing vexation to others.
Furthermore, to intentionally perform a formal declaration (*jñapti*) is termed "causing vexation to others"; the determination of the offense follows the previous rule.
This constitutes the combined formulation of two precepts.
Thirteenth: To revile or scold a monk appointed by *karmavācanā* as an administrator constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.

According to the Vinaya, reviling someone where one sees them but does not hear them is termed "slandering" (*ūnavāda*); reviling someone where one hears them but does not see them is termed "scolding" (*akkosa*). These two precepts are established together.
Fourteenth: The offense of spreading monastic woolen rugs or mats in an open, unenclosed space.
If one intends to return quickly and departs for only a brief moment, there is no offense.
However, if the intention is to depart permanently, the offense is incurred the moment one steps through the door.
Fifteenth, the offense of spreading out bedding in a secluded place:
if one intends to depart permanently, the offense is incurred the moment one crosses the boundary;
if one intends to depart temporarily, the offense is incurred at the appearance of the dawn-light on the third night.
The sixteenth: knowing that another is staying in a place, to later forcibly spread bedding there to harass them constitutes an offense.
"Creating such a cause and condition" refers to the condition of harassing another.
"Non-other" means it is not one of the other permitted exceptions.
"Non-dignified" means losing the deportment of a great person according to the monastic discipline. Seventeenth:
the offense of forcibly leading another out of a spring or winter residence.
If one drags another out of a room during the summer retreat when that room belongs to oneself, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
This is because the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* contains a precept against dragging others out of their rooms during the summer retreat, for which a *bhikṣu* commits a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, section fourteen, states: "If one drives out a snake or a rat out of anger, it is a violation of the Vinaya.
However, if one thinks:
"This is a useless creature; there is no offense in driving it out," [there is no transgression].
18. Regarding sitting on a high multi-storied building with a bed whose legs can be drawn out: this is an offense because it may injure those below.
19. The precept concerning the use of water containing insects.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sa-po-tuo lun), fascicle six, states: "Śāriputra, using his purified divine eye, saw insects in the air as numerous as the sands in water—boundless and immeasurable—and he abstained from food for two or three days."
The Buddha commanded that they eat.
Generally, the regulation regarding water containing insects is based on what is visible to the naked eye.
One should filter the water and have those who uphold the precepts, are learned, have deep faith in the consequences of karma, and are composed and discerning, determine whether the water is clear.
Filter it according to the Dharma and place it in a vessel sufficient for one day’s use; examine it again the following day.
If there are insects, one should filter it thoroughly and then, using a clean vessel filled with water, gaze at it intently toward the sun.
If there are still insects present, one should strain with a double-layered filter.
If they are still present, one should use a triple-layered filter.
If they are still present, one should move away quickly.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 15, states: "The appearance of these insects is not constant; they may have been absent previously and then appear, or they may have been present previously and now be gone. For this reason, a bhikṣu should examine [the water] attentively every day, and only use it when no insects are found."
The rest is largely the same as in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*.
The Tripiṭaka Master Rāhula is currently before our eyes.
However, he takes fine silk and dyes it until it is thoroughly processed; as for raw silk, insects may pass through it, so one should verify this for oneself.
Furthermore, one must use a fine thread to mark two lines, ensuring that when threading the needle, no holes are made so as not to allow insects to escape.

Once the strainer has been set up, when pouring water, one should place the jar inside the strainer and draw the water out slowly and steadily. After drawing the water, one must rinse the jar with clean water two or three times to ensure it is thoroughly purified.
Once the exterior has been rinsed, rinse the interior of the jar as well before setting it on the ground.
Take the water that has been strained and place it in a new lacquered vessel, then set it upright upon a stand.
Alternatively, one may construct a separate water-observation platform and, covering the mouth with the hand, observe it for a long time.
If insects are seen, filter the water again according to the proper method; once filtered, turn the strainer inside out and place it into the release-vessel.
The efficacy of the jar-method has been personally verified, though I lack the leisure to describe it in full detail.
When the jar is lowered into the well, it must be submerged and withdrawn several times before being pulled out.

If the net is shaken at the top of the well, the resulting upward splashing and downward surging will inevitably harm the lives of insects; those who delight in protecting living beings should therefore pay close attention to this matter.
The Tripitaka Master said:
"At times, some make small circular strainers that hold only one *sheng* or two *he*.

Since they are made of coarse, thin silk, they do not actually observe insects; yet they hang them beside their bowls for others to see. Having no intention to protect life, they incur faults day after day; therefore, this is not permissible."
Twenty: The precept against inspecting a roof that has been repaired more than three times.
Examining the intent of the Vinaya, the "three layers" refers to a triple-layered roof.
This was established as a prohibition because such heavy roofing causes the dwelling to collapse and invites public censure.
If one observes two layers of covering and reaches three but has not yet finished, the bhikṣu must distance himself from the place where he can be seen or heard; otherwise, he commits an offense.
Regarding "doors, windows, and casements," etc., these distinguish the characteristics of the building; they do not intend to distinguish the nature of the offense.

The twenty-first: According to the Vinaya, nuns are required to request a person to provide instruction every half-month; if there is a bhikṣu endowed with the ten virtues who accepts the nuns' request.
At that time, the Saṃgha was required to formally appoint a teacher for the nuns through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
Now, to go and teach the nuns without having been so appointed constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.
This principle has already been briefly explained above in the introduction to the precepts.
Twenty-second: A monk appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct nuns may do so until sunset; this was established because his actions invited public censure.

Twenty-third: If the group of six bhikṣus, upon seeing a virtuous person appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct nuns, out of envy deride him by saying, "He does this for the sake of greed for profit," they commit an offense.
Twenty-fifth: The precept regarding making robes. This constitutes an offense with every stitch; the details are as explained in the Vinaya.
Twenty-sixth: The precept regarding sitting in a secluded place with a nun.
If there is a wise layman acting as a third person, there is no offense.
Twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth: Traveling by the same boat according to a prior agreement.
The Vinaya states: "If one has not previously made an agreement with another, and they happen to meet on the road, one should proceed with caution and not venture to travel together."
The Buddha said:
"If it was not intentionally sought, there is no offense.
The twenty-ninth: The precept against eating food praised by a nun.
If one knows that a nun has praised her own virtues to cause a donor to prepare food, one commits an offense.

If the donor has already prepared the food themselves, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there is no offense provided one did not praise [her]; likewise, there is no offense if one was unaware of the praise.
Thirty-first: A donor constructs a "merit-hall" (puṇya-śālā) and limits it to providing one meal for one overnight guest; if one accepts more than this, an offense is committed.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 16, states: "Construct a house of sixteen bays, with one bay assigned to each family."
"If one has accepted [the invitation] in full, one should depart for one night; thereafter, one may return again, and this constitutes successive acceptance.
According to the Vinaya, if a donor understands that a sick person is suffering, accepting more than the prescribed limit does not constitute an offense.
The thirty-second precept concerns eating in succession:

if one has been invited by a previous household for the five kinds of formal meals and has accepted that invitation, yet turns away from them to accept the five kinds of formal meals from a subsequent household and eats at that latter household, there is an offense of *pāyattika* for every swallow.
To reject what was received before and accept what was received later is called "successive rejection" (*krama*).
If one rejects food that is insufficient, improper, impure, and so forth, because the mental transgression is slight, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, while eating at a later household, one eats improper food, insufficient food, impure food, or does not eat at all, and the donor hears of it but does not give rise to grave resentment, it is likewise only a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the phrase "except at other times," this refers to excluding those times when an exception is permitted.
There are two textual openings for these exceptions, which are expanded into three meanings, and reach four when the principles are fully exhausted.
As for the two mentioned: first, the time of illness; second, the time of the distribution of robes.
Regarding the "three [circumstances]," the first is the time of illness.
This illness must be such that one is unable to eat or drink; even if excellent food is obtained, one cannot consume it—it is only then that one is within the permitted limit.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "For one who is ill and unable to eat while remaining seated, one should provide sufficient choice food.
Regarding the second [occasion], the time for giving robes, according to the Vinaya texts, it is divided into two types:

first, the month of Kārttika following the conclusion of the earlier *anuvassa* (rainy-season retreat), or the five months during which the *kaṭhina* robe has been accepted; within this period, it is the time for receiving gifts, and is thus called the "time for giving robes."

Second, even if it is not within the period of one month or five months, if at any other time a donor offers food or robes, it is permitted to reject the former and accept the latter; this is called the "time for receiving robes."
Because the previous illness was permitted, there are thus three permissions.

As for the mention of "four," this adds the permission regarding the abandonment of an invitation; that is to say, if one wishes to reject a prior invitation to accept a meal at a later house, one should abandon the prior invitation.
As the Vinaya text states: "Venerable One!
I ought to go there; I now bestow it upon you.
This is the scriptural passage concerning the formal relinquishment [of the object].
One should speak fully thus:
"Venerable sir!
Today I have accepted an invitation from the donor, the Zhang family, from the lanes and alleys of that neighborhood."
"I ought to go there; I now bestow this upon you.
According to this Vinaya text, when giving to another person, that person must go to receive the meal from the donor (*dānapati*); only when both parties benefit is it considered non-offensive.
This differs from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which prescribes merely maintaining mindfulness as a precaution at dawn.
Therefore, practitioners of old have interpreted the meaning of the "Six Mindfulnesses" (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) of the *Mahāsāṃghika* within the context of this precept.
According to the sixteenth fascicle of that *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the meaning should be understood as follows:

at the first thought-moment, one should recollect whether this month is large or small, whether it is the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, and count the days—whether the first, second, third, or so on—in accordance with their number.

This mental recitation generally discusses black and white [actions] to distinguish between the great and the small; if one calculates by days, they are divided into one, two, and so forth according to whether they are black or white.
Regarding the second recitation, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it says:
"The food I have received today, I shall give to such-and-such a person."
"Regarding me, [the donor] does not calculate [the recipient as 'I']; I shall eat. This is stated three times.

Now, as for the intent of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: regarding whatever food one is to receive during the course of a single day, one should beforehand at dawn perform the ritual of "purification by declaration" (*śuddhivācanā*), mentally reflecting and verbally declaring that it is given to the five groups of renunciants.
Therefore, the meaning of the passage is: "The food I have received today I shall give to such-and-such a śrāmaṇera;
that śrāmaṇera will not harbor expectations toward me, for he does not begrudge me this food."
The same applies to giving to a great bhikṣu; it should be explained according to this principle.
"I shall eat" means one should form the perception that one is eating the food of that śrāmaṇera or others.
According to this, if one falsely relinquishes [the food] to another person, [it constitutes an offense].
If others do not attend and the donor’s preparations are in vain, this does not accord with the essential requirement of this Vinaya for actual relinquishment (*pratyākhyāna*).

Therefore, according to this Vinaya, because mindfulness (*smṛti*) prevents non-comprehension, when performing the mindfulness, one merely intends to remember and know that one should perform the relinquishment of the invitation (*pravāraṇā*). Thus, one should mindfully recite: "The second mindfulness: I do not turn my back on the invited food."

As for the time of the midday meal, if there are many invitations and one intends to decline them, one must specifically relinquish those invitations; this should be understood as previously explained.
If there is a reason of illness, one should say:
"At the second thought-moment, I have a reason of illness and must decline the invitation to eat."

Other conditions are to be understood by analogy with this. Thirdly, one should record the year, such as the *jiǎzǐ* or *yǐchǒu* sexagenary cycle; the first month, such as the *yǐchǒu* new moon; the second day, such as the *jiǎzǐ*; and the time, such as the *jǐngwēn* (noon) *yǐn* hour, when the shadow of a one-foot wooden gnomon was two feet long. Having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), one should state the number of summer retreats (*varṣa*)—such as zero, one, or two—and the length of the shadow at that specific time, whether it be *zi*, *chǒu*, or any other hour, according to the actual measurement. One, two, or more years of summer retreats are likewise to be stated accordingly.
If, at the time of receiving the precepts, it is cloudy and there is no sun, one should simply say:
"I receive the full ordination during the first watch of the morning. The middle and latter watches should be referred to accordingly.
Regarding the fourth mindfulness, if the three robes and bowl are not complete, one should say:
"The *saṃghāṭī* and *uttarāsaṅga* are already complete; the *antarvāsaka* is not yet complete, and I shall procure it.
[In this manner,] mention whichever other robes or bowl are lacking.
Whether one has already received and maintained [the robes] or not, in accordance with those who have not yet maintained them, one says:
"The saṃghāṭī has not been received and maintained; I shall now receive and maintain it.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
If one *dīrghacīvara* has already been formally dedicated (*viśuddha*), but one or two sections have not yet been formally dedicated, one should say:
"This garment has not yet been formally dedicated; I shall now perform its formal dedication. The remaining garments have already been formally dedicated."
Fifth, regarding the mindfulness of not eating separately from the community (*pṛthag-bhakta*), or when there is a reason for eating separately, one should say:
"I have the reason of illness; I shall eat separately from the community.
Other reasons should be stated accordingly.
The sixth reflection is: "I am currently free from illness. If one is practicing in reliance upon the community, should there be circumstances of illness, one should say:
"I am currently ill and shall receive medical treatment.

The first reflection is for the purpose of knowing the date and time for the recitation of the precepts; furthermore, one should reflect on impermanence, how days and months pass away, and cultivate weariness with and detachment from birth and death.
The second mindfulness is to prevent causing distress to the donor;
the third mindfulness is to prevent the affliction of arrogance and also to prevent the offense of theft;
the fourth mindfulness is to cultivate distinct practices in accordance with the teachings.
The fifth mindfulness is to follow the practice of harmony;
the sixth mindfulness is to follow the practice of non-negligence so that all deeds are accomplished.
According to the Vinaya, to turn one's back on the former constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, while to turn one's back on the latter constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.

That is to say, if one accepts ten invitations and then turns away from the first invitation to accept food at the remaining nine households, for every swallow of food between those instances, one commits one *pāyattika* offense and eight *dukkaṭa* offenses.
Since only the first house constitutes the prior invitation (*pūrva-nimantraṇa*), while the remaining nine houses are all subsequent invitations (*paścāt-nimantraṇa*),
if one turns away from the second house and eats at the first house, there is a fault for every swallow, amounting to nine transgressions.
The thirty-third: The precept against eating in a separate group.
This refers to cases where, within a natural or formally established boundary (sīmā), one singles out specific monks for an invitation or solicits food separately from them.
In this case, at a place where four or more people are eating, if one excludes other monks— even down to a single person—
and eats the five types of formal meals during that time, then with every swallow, one commits the offense of eating separately from the community (*pṛthag-bhojana*).
If one invites the Sangha for a meal, four persons may eat together without committing the offense of eating separately, as the flavors of the food are the same.

According to the intent of the Vinaya regulations, this is because: first, there is concern that evil persons might form factions to disrupt the Sangha; and second, there is concern that it would become difficult to provide for the Sangha’s donors. Therefore, only three or fewer persons are permitted [to eat separately].

According to the explanatory sections on exemptions in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, there are seven exemptions, which can be expanded into eight; when taken to their logical conclusion, there are fourteen.
Regarding the seven exemptions: first is "illness," where this illness extends down to a split heel such that one cannot keep pace with one's companions while walking.
Second, "the time for making robes" refers to the month of Kārttika and the five months during which the *kaṭhina* robe is in effect; this is the proper time for making robes.
Third, "the time for the offering of robes" allows for two types, as distinguished in the preceding precepts.
Question:
If the time for giving robes is also one month or five months, how does it differ from the time for making robes?
Answer:
In this case, the action is the same while the circumstances differ; thus, opening [the robe] into two parts incurs no fault.

Regarding "the time of making the robe": when one originally received the cloth, the intention was to make a robe. Thereafter, as long as one constantly maintains the intent to make the robe—even until one makes the "horse-tooth" (stitch) seam upon the cloth—one does not lose the benefit.
If, however, during this interval one's intention to make the robe is interrupted, one immediately loses the five benefits.

Regarding the "time of receiving the offered robe": when there is no specific formal intention, but one directly accepts the benefits for a period of one month or five months, this time of acceptance is called the "time of receiving the offered robe."
Only when the limit is reached does one lose the five benefits.
Fourth, "when traveling on foot," refers to a distance of at least half a yojana.
Fifth, "when riding in a boat," likewise extends to half a yojana.
Sixth, "When the Great Assembly Gathers": During the beginning and end of the summer retreat, when people from all quarters assemble to pay their respects, food is difficult to obtain.
Since a donor’s mental effort can provide for four people but not five, this [rule] is thus relaxed.
7. Regarding "the śramaṇa’s distribution of food": this refers to non-Buddhist śramaṇas who limit their offerings to four people and cannot extend them to five.
Out of consideration for their intentions, they are also included within the permitted limit.
Regarding the statement "eight," this refers to the two [categories] concerning the gift of robes.

Regarding the statement "fourteen," according to the seventh fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, there are five types of non-offenses; adding these to the previous thirteen, and including the one from this present Vinaya, they total fourteen.

Regarding the "five": first, if one strikes the bell and does not stop [the meal], there is no offense; however, if one stops the meal for the Sangha, one commits the offense of stealing communal property, and if one stops the meal offered as a gift, one commits the offense of eating separately from the assembly.
If one calls out "those with sixty years of seniority" when entering [the hall], there is no offense.

This refers to a case where a donor intends to make a long-term invitation for ninety days, but their resources do not extend that far; in such a case, one should strike the chime on the first day and announce, "Those with sixty years of seniority, enter."
If even a single person enters, the others all remain free from offense.
If there is no one with sixty years of seniority, the number may be gradually reduced as they announce it, until no one remains; even if a single śrāmaṇera enters, there is no offense.
If it is not announced on the first day, it must be announced every day.
Third, there is no offense if one is invited according to the monastic order (*saṃghakrama*).

This refers to two or three locations within the same boundary; even if one receives an invitation from the monastic order for as few as a single person to come and eat together, no offense is incurred for the others.
The sequence of monks outside the boundary is likewise of no benefit.
Fourth, there is no offense in sending food to the Sangha.

Whether at the place of invitation or the place of begging, if one takes out a portion of food and sends it into the midst of the Sangha to be distributed as alms to the monks, there is no offense whatsoever.
Fifth, there is no offense if one sets aside food with the intention of returning it later.

The *Śāstra* states: "If one is not invited according to the monastic order, one should set aside a portion of food at the head of the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) with the intention of presenting it to the Saṃgha."
"If there are monks who are unable to carry [the food], one should take this food and distribute it in order.

Furthermore, according to this Vinaya, there is another provision for relaxation, stating: "If there are four people or more than four, they should divide into two groups and enter the meal area alternately."
This, together with the preceding [rules], constitutes fourteen permissions.

Regarding the thirty-fourth precept, which prohibits taking more than three bowlfuls of a practitioner’s provisions: according to the Vinaya texts, there was a case where a woman intending to return to her husband prepared provisions for the journey; however, because the bhikṣu begged excessively and she could not return in time, the husband abandoned her.
Furthermore, there were merchants traveling with provisions when a bhikṣu approached them for alms; this caused the merchants to fall behind their caravan and be plundered by bandits.

Therefore, these items are all the food and supplies of travelers; if one takes them while passing by just before departure, it constitutes an offense, except in cases of illness, where it is permitted.
Why must this necessarily refer only to a returning wife or a guest?
Furthermore, it is incorrect for Nanshan to state that "this matter is rare and therefore not explained extensively.
Moreover, according to the Vinaya texts, from one bhikṣu up to five bhikṣus, there is an offense in each case according to their respective order.
For example, if the first bhikṣu eats at that house and, having finished eating, brings back four bowls of food, then that first person commits an offense.
If, however, after this bhikṣu has finished eating, he takes three bowls and goes to the monastery to divide them and eat together with others, then this person has not committed an offense.
There was a second person who wished to go for alms, and the first bhikṣu said to that person going:
"I have finished eating; bring three [portions] back.
If you go, simply eat there, and be careful not to bring anything back."
When that person has finished eating, they nevertheless take one more; this is the second person’s offense.

If the first person finishes eating and takes two, and the second person finishes eating and takes one, and they both divide them to eat together, they tell the third person: "Go there to eat, but be careful not to bring anything back.
When that third person finishes eating and takes one, this is the third person’s offense.

If the first person finishes eating and takes one [portion], and the second and third persons likewise each take one upon finishing their meals, they divide them all and eat; they then tell the fourth person to go and eat without taking any portion.
When that fourth person finishes eating and takes one [portion], it is the fourth person who commits the offense.

If the first person finishes eating and does not take [the portion], and the second, third, and fourth persons each go to eat and then each take one portion, and they all divide and eat it together, while telling the fifth person to go eat but not to take [a portion];
yet the fifth person goes and takes [it], then the fifth person commits an offense.
However, according to the Vinaya texts, if one carries [food] beyond the limit and crosses the threshold with both feet outside the door, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one carries three portions back to the monastery and eats them without distributing them, one commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.
As for the statement in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* that "it does not constitute a *pācittiya* offense," this is an interpretation of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
According to the Vinaya, upon arriving at a donor’s house, one should ask what kind of food it is.

Regarding the thirty-fifth precept on "eating after having finished" (*khalupaścādbhaktika*), the text states "having finished eating" (*bhuktavān*); this refers to having finished eating the five types of regular staple foods (*pañca bhojanāni*) belonging to the monastery, or having finished eating the five types of staple foods belonging to oneself.
"Sometimes accepting an invitation" means having finished eating the five kinds of formal meals at the invitation of a donor (*dānapati*).
These two phrases clarify that one has already sat down and completed the meal.

"To eat while not performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* (the ritual for leftover food) constitutes an offense" means that after having eaten the five kinds of formal meals before noon, if one wishes to eat again, one ought to perform the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* ritual.

If one eats without performing the ritual formalities (*karmavācanā*) and simply consumes the food, then with every swallow, one commits the offense of *pācittiya* for having finished eating (*pūtimukta*).
There are three meanings of "finished" (*pūti*):
first, it must consist of the five types of solid food (*bhojana*); if it is not the five types of solid food, then the meaning of "finished" does not apply.
Second, one eats until fully satiated;
third, although not yet completely full, this proper meal is sufficient to sustain one for a day—this is what is called "sufficiency of the object.
When sitting before the meal, once the eating is finished, one rises and alters one's posture.
Whether it be satiety with food or satiety with sensory objects, if one eats again thereafter without performing the remaining ritual procedures, there is an offense of *pācittiya* for every swallow.
This applies equally whether one is eating while walking, standing, or lying down; once the posture has changed, the same rule should be observed accordingly.

The five types of formal food (*bhojana*) are: first, thick rice gruel—when it first comes out of the cauldron, if one draws a line with a blade of grass and it does not adhere, it is also categorized as rice; second, parched flour; third, dry rice; fourth, fish; and fifth, meat.

Regarding the ritual for leftover food (*khalupaścādbhaktavidhi*): if one wishes to eat again, one should have a *śramaṇera* or a lay attendant take up some food intended for eating. Whether it is poured from a regular vessel or an improper vessel, it must be pure and not contaminated by remnants or contact with impurities; the bhikṣu then washes his hands and receives it from the attendant.
Once the meal has been received, one should seek out those who have not yet arrived and sit before them until they are finished.

A bhikṣu acts as the object for another; if that person is still eating, one must not alter one’s posture. If one alters it, the meal is considered finished, and one may no longer act as the object for the other.
Facing this person and holding the food according to the proper ritual, one says:
"Venerable One!
I have finished eating; know this and take note of it."
Having spoken these words regarding the ritual for leftover food (*kṛta-pātra-śeṣa-dharma*), he hands it to the person before him.
The meaning of the text here is that he intends for the other to understand his purpose: "Take this from me; after eating a small portion, leave the remainder as a remnant."
That bhikṣu, having taken a small amount of food, should say to the other bhikṣu:
"Take as much food as you wish.
Furthermore, there is a textual passage that says: "I shall stop; you take and eat it."
The Vinaya text on the seven-day medicine states: "One should say to them:
'Cease your greed for food.'"
The thirty-sixth precept: Exhorting against eating after having finished one's meal.
The text states, "knowing that another has already finished eating," which means knowing that the monastic community or an individual has already finished their meal.
If it refers to one who has accepted an invitation, it means the donor has already finished eating.
These two cases conclude with the rule regarding eating to satiety; they are explained according to the preceding precept.

Regarding "advising [a monk] without having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of remaining food)": this is because, once the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* has been performed, one may advise [another] without committing an offense.
"By these causes and conditions" refers to the causal conditions of exhorting with an evil mind.
"Not otherwise" means that it is not the case that other circumstances constitute a non-offense.
That is to say, if one performs other acts—such as [giving] the remains of a sick person, or exhorting when that bhikṣu is ill—one does not commit an offense.
The thirty-seventh: The precept against eating at improper times.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "After midday, no material substance whatsoever may be placed within the mouth."
"After eating, one should use a tooth-stick or rinse the mouth with ashes; otherwise, there is an offense of falling [into a transgression].
According to this, once the meal is finished under the precept regarding "having had enough," if one changes one's posture but has not yet rinsed the mouth, there is an offense for every swallow.
If one enters the afternoon, with every swallow of food, one incurs the offense of eating at an improper time (*vikālabhojana*).

Thirty-eighth: Regarding leftover food from the previous night (*paryuṣita-śeṣa-bhakṣa*): if food received on this day reaches until the appearance of the dawn light of the following day, it is called "leftover from the previous night."
The thirty-ninth precept: The Precept Against Accepting Food.
Regarding the phrase "except for water and tooth-sticks," if turbid water or tooth-sticks require that one swallow their liquid residue, this is permitted within the scope of the allowance.
Fortieth: The Precept Against Soliciting Delicate Food.

According to the principles of renunciation, one ought to abandon all exquisite flavors; yet, craving and seeking fine food increases afflictions and augments greed. The conditions for its transgression consist of four factors: [1] the object, which is delicious food; [2] the perception, which is the recognition of it as such; [3] the intention, which is the desire to obtain it; and [4] the action, which is the act of soliciting it.
First, fine food; second, for oneself; third, without cause; fourth, eating constitutes an offense.
The precept text has three parts:
first, the person who commits the offense; second, the enumeration of the four kinds of fine food; third, the formal definition of the offense.

Next, citing the conditions for exemption, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 8, states: "If one seeks [food] on behalf of a sick bhikṣu, whether from the home of a relative or from those such as acquaintances, there is no offense in any case."
Forty-first: The precept against giving food to non-Buddhists.
It is said that one commits an offense if one gives with one's own hand; however, there is no offense if one causes another person to give it or places it on the ground for them.
Forty-second: Having accepted an invitation, one must not enter a village before or after a meal without having informed [another monk].
Regarding the phrase "before or after a meal" in the text of the precept, the Sanskrit original is inverted; the phrasing should be corrected to "before the meal or after the meal."
According to the Vinaya, "before the meal" refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until the time for the midday meal;
"after the meal" refers to the period from after the midday meal until noon.

Entering a village after noon constitutes an offense under the rule against entering a settlement at an improper time (*vikāla-gāma-praveśa-śikṣāpada*), and is not subsumed under this particular precept.
"Visiting another household" means not going to the house where one has been invited, but instead proceeding to another household.
If one intends to go there, it is not an offense provided one informs another person of one's departure.
According to this precept, there are four sections in the opening text, which, when fully analyzed according to principle, amount to five.
As for the four, the first is entrusting [the robe] to another bhikṣu.
According to tradition from ancient times, at the time of entrusting, one should say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], having previously accepted an invitation from [Name], now have a certain matter for which I wish to enter a certain village and go to a certain house before the meal. I inform the Venerable sir so that he may know."
He replied, “It may be so.
After the meal, he informed [the Buddha]; this may be understood accordingly.
Now, upon careful examination, it is simply necessary to clearly instruct those who know [the procedure], so that they may remember and uphold it well.
One must seek out a knowledgeable person; it is not strictly required to use such phrases as "Venerable Sir, please attend to me" (*bhadante ekāgramanāḥ śṛṇu*).
Second, when one is ill; third, when making robes; fourth, when robes are being offered.

Within the occasion of robes being offered, two sub-categories are established; following the explanation above regarding the rule on successive meals, these constitute five occasions of dispensation in total.

The forty-third precept: "There is treasure in the house of one who provides food. This refers to men and women who, being mutually attracted, each give rise to craving for the other's taste; in meaning, this is equivalent to [craving] for food.
If one does not sever the conditions of craving, the object of one's affection is equivalent in significance to a treasure.
This refers to the offense committed when a bhikṣu forcibly sits down while a husband and wife are engaged in mutual passion, thereby obstructing their sexual act.
If there is a wise man acting as the fourth person, there is no offense.
Master Nanshan says this constitutes "contact-food" (*sparśāhāra*);
this is truly laughable.

The forty-fourth precept states: regarding a household where there is a husband who is a man of wealth, even though the husband is absent, if a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place where he cannot reach the door with his hands, such that outsiders cannot see him, it constitutes an offense.
If there is a third person present, there is no offense.

Regarding the forty-fifth precept concerning sitting in the open with a woman, the *Vinaya* commentary on the definition of "a secluded place" states that it refers to both a place where one can see in seclusion and a place where one can hear in seclusion; it is designated as "open" because it lacks a roof.

Furthermore, being "in private" (*praticchanna*) refers to a place where one is neither seen nor heard; since it is already an offense even in such a secluded place, it must also be an offense when there is concealment (*paticchādana*), for this meaning inherently includes both concealment and privacy.
This precept applies to women regardless of whether they are monastics or laypeople;
there is no distinction between them. If there is a third person present, there is no offense.
The forty-sixth precept: harboring feelings of resentment from the past, one lures another into a village, saying that one intends to give her food.
He then secretly invited [the monks] to his home, but when the appointed time arrived, he drove them out of the settlement, saying, "You lack merit; you will not obtain food.
It was due to this cause and condition of causing such distress that the offense was committed.
The forty-seventh precept: Knowing that another has invited one to receive medicine for a period of four months, to accept it beyond that limit when not ill constitutes an offense.
If one is ill, there is no offense.
"Permanent invitation" (nitya-nimantraṇā) refers to the fact that the intention to give is not limited [by time].
"Repeated invitation" (punar-nimantraṇā) refers to the re-invitation for a period of four months.
"Shared invitation" (vibhakta-nimantraṇā) refers to the fact that although the medicine is divided, there is no limitation on the time.
"Throughout one's life" means either until the end of the donor's life or until the end of the bhikṣu's life.
Forty-eighth: Regarding "observing an army," this constitutes an offense whether it be for the purpose of viewing military maneuvers or military combat.
Regarding "except in cases of timely causes and conditions": if one has been invited or must perform a formal announcement (*jñapti*), it is permitted to see [the army] without committing an offense.
Forty-ninth: if there is a reason to go to an army, one should depart from a place where one can see or hear [the soldiers] by the third night, before the light of dawn has appeared.
Fifty: There are three circumstances regarding staying overnight; one should settle the mind in tranquility and not observe a battle.
Fifty-one: The precept against drinking alcohol.
To drink alcohol while perceiving it as such, or while suspecting it to be so, constitutes a *pāyattika*.

The fifty-second [offense]: According to the Vinaya, even playing by scooping water with a bowl constitutes a *duṣkṛta*; if one scoops curd, thin gruel, or other liquids from a vessel, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.

The fifty-fourth [offense]: When one is about to commit a transgression and refuses to accept admonition or restraint, upon committing the original offense, there is added the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of "refusing admonition."
Fifty-sixth: The Precept on Bathing.

The text states, "one must not exceed," meaning one must not exceed the prohibition established by the Buddha that bathing occurs no less frequently than once every half-month; it does not mean that one must bathe exactly once every half-month and may not bathe later than that.
There are six exceptions to this precept.

First, regarding "the time of heat": according to the Vinaya, this refers to forty-five days of spring plus the first month of summer, that is, from the first day of the third month to the middle of the fifth month, totaling two and a half months.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 8, states: "Because it is hot early in India, this period is chosen.
Thus, according to the time when it becomes hot in each respective location, one may count two and a half months; bathing during this interval constitutes no offense.
2. "When ill" refers to even the point where one's own body emits a foul odor.
3. "When working" refers to even the point of sweeping the ground in front of one's house.
4. "When there is wind" refers to even the occurrence of a single whirlwind.
5. Regarding "during the rainy season," it means even a single drop of rain falls upon the body.
6. Regarding "long journey," it refers to half a yojana.
Fifty-seventh: The Precept on Kindling Fire.

Regarding the phrase "except in cases of timely circumstances," according to the Vinaya, it is not only the act of cooking over an open flame that constitutes an offense; even if it is not cooking over an open flame, one still commits a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
Therefore, the Vinaya provides exceptions for timely circumstances, meaning that for a sick bhikṣu, there is no offense in boiling soup or rice, or even in dyeing robes and so forth.
If one refrains from committing such an act in private, how can one not be guilty when openly damaging the ground?
It is clearly understood that even for one who is not ill, refraining in private still constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
According to the Vinaya teachings regarding lighting a lamp, one should say: "Look at this; know this.
The fifty-ninth precept concerns taking what has been offered as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) without first inquiring about it.

To speak generally regarding the mind: a person of few desires possesses the very foundation for nurturing the Way; therefore, the Buddha strictly prescribed that one should possess only the three robes.
Regarding all requisites and conditions beyond these three robes, one should cultivate the perception of them as being for others, just as in the practice of the meditative gateways.
There are two types in total:

first, actual mental attention (*bhūtamanasikāra*), such as the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*), which takes real breath-wind and so forth as its object; second, conceptual mental attention (*parikalpitamanasikāra*), such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), which conceptually constructs a person who has died and then analyzes the corpse.
Both of these gateways of contemplation are capable of counteracting afflictions.
Now, this "pure giving" (*śuddhadāna*) also involves forming a mental image of having completed the act of giving to another, thereby conceiving of the object as belonging to another.
It is called pure giving because it serves to counteract the defilement of greed and attachment toward one's own possessions and requisites.
The World-Honored One has established excellent regulations; how could one disregard them and fail to practice?

According to the Vinaya, a "pure gift" (śuddha-dāna) must involve inviting a donor; this refers to obtaining an extra article and giving it to another person, designating that person as the owner, which is why they are called a "donor."
There are two kinds of donors:
first, the truly pure donor, as stated in this precept text: "to the five assemblies, such as bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs";
second, the indirect pure donor, as explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*: "all surplus property must be purified by means of the five assemblies."

One should seek out a donor who maintains the precepts, is learned, and possesses virtue; subsequently, having obtained goods, one should perform the *śuddhi* (purification) rite by reciting the name of the *śuddhi*-master before a single bhikṣu.
If the pure master dies or departs for another country, one should seek another pure master.
When requesting these two kinds of pure masters, one should perform the ritual with these words:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!"
I, the bhikṣu [Name], now request the Venerable One to act as my *bhūta-śuddhi-dānapati* (true pure donor) or *paramparā-śuddhi-dānapati* (successive pure donor).
May the Venerable One act for me as my *bhūta-śuddhi-dānapati*, out of compassion. (Recite this three times.)
"Successive pure donors should be understood accordingly.
[The text] explains the two types of pure donors according to the invitation.
If one intends to perform a "true purification" (*bhūta-pariśuddhi*), one should stand before the donor with full decorum, hold the robe in hand, and say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!

I have this one long robe, or two or three robes, etc., as measured; they have not yet been purified through formal assignment (*pariṣkāra*). Now, for the sake of purification, I relinquish them to you, Venerable sir, for the purpose of true purification. Since the Vinaya does not state that the formula must be recited three times, it is known that a single recitation suffices."
"This text is from the *Cīvara-vastu* (Chapter on Robes), which is superior to the explanations found in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Having performed this ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), the object is entrusted to the donor;
if it must later be worn or used, one may do so only after having asked the donor's permission.
To put on [the robe] without asking [permission] causes the donor to become fearful and lose their garment; since this constitutes an act of harassment toward them, it was therefore prohibited.
Second, as for the practice of "successive purification" (*kṣetra-śuddhi*), this is what is commonly practiced today, so I shall not describe it here at length.

Regarding the two types of purification (*pariśuddhi*), it is called "actual" (*bhūta*) because the object is personally entrusted to the recipient; it does not mean that one must mentally resolve to definitely give the object to that person.

However, according to the Vinaya and Śāstras, both types of purifiers are listed among the five groups of monastics. Regarding this, ancient discussions have held that the actual purifier must perform the ritual within the assembly (*saṃgha*) and personally entrust the object, for if a monk were to entrust it to a nun, or a nun to a monk, it would incur public censure and defilement at the time of the exchange.

Regarding this indirect purification (*pariśuddhi*), since one does not personally face the pure master (*viśuddha-adhipati*) before them, there is no impediment to monks and nuns acting for one another.

Furthermore, according to the texts of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when declaring the purity of an indirect gift, it is not permitted to do so in the presence of that donor; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Regarding the aforementioned property, even if it measures only one chi, six cun, or eight cun, regardless of whether it is new or old, internal or external, pure or impure, it must all be rendered *pariśuddha* (purified).
Sixtieth: The Precept on White Garments.
*Kāṣāya* is translated in this region as "not correct" (*bùzhèng*).

Furthermore, since the text of the precepts speaks of three kinds of dyed colors (*trividha-kāṣāya*), we know that deep blue and deep black are subsumed under the five primary colors (*pañca-varṇa*), and are not included within the "blue and black" mentioned in the precept text.
Therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, fascicle eight, states: "Regarding the five primary colors, if one dyes them oneself, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one makes robes from them, they cannot be properly received and maintained."
It further states: "The five primary colors are yellow, red, blue, black, and white. It also says:
"If it is not pure blue, light blue, or turquoise, one may perform the ritual of 'spot-purification' (pindoddhāra) and use it for the lining of a robe."
According to this Vinaya, a white [mark] constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense, while failing to dot it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, eighteen [khandhakas], a white [mark] constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense, while failing to dot it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.

Therefore, within that Vinaya, it is permitted to perform the ritual of *parikamma* (purification by marking) using dark blue; thus, the text states, "Blue refers to indigo. This is shown to distinguish it from other colors, fearing that people might use them indiscriminately.
According to various Vinayas and śāstras, when performing the ritual marking (*pradakṣiṇa*), one should make one, three, five, seven, or nine marks; they must not be made in pairs.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the mark should be at most the size of four fingers and at least the size of a pea.
The sixty-third: The precept against causing others doubt and distress.
This refers to using skillful means to cause another bhikṣu to suspect that he has violated the precepts or to suspect that he lacks the precepts, with the intent of causing him distress.

Even if one’s intention is merely to cause another momentary displeasure, the offense of *pāyattika* is incurred as soon as the other person hears and knows of it; it does not require that the other actually experience momentary displeasure before the offense is committed.

Sixty-fourth: Concealing a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). The two categories of *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, along with the offenses of shedding blood and causing a schism in the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*), are termed "grave offenses."
If one conceals [the offense] until the appearance of the dawn light, one commits a *thullaccaya* (offense of grave misconduct).
Sixty-fifth: Acting as an upādhyāya (preceptor) for one who has not reached the required age for ordination.
If one knows [the person is underage] or suspects it, both commit a *thullaccaya*; the other teachers and monks commit a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
The matter of receiving the precepts is of great importance; since it prevents others from obtaining them and imposes heavy responsibility upon the preceptor and the Sangha, it is deeply censurable.
Sixty-sixth: The Precept Against Inciting Dispute.

There are four kinds of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*): those concerning accusations, searching for faults, offenses, and matters pertaining to the Saṃgha; these are subsumed within the four disputes. To initiate an offense that constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) is [to engage in] a dispute over an offense; however, if one initiates a dispute through mere idle talk, it is merely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
"Repenting according to the Dharma" means to extinguish [the offense] by means of the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
These seven methods settle the four types of disputes, which will be explained below in the section on the Seven Rules for Settling Disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha-vinaya*).
[The sixty-eighth case concerns] one who claims that desire does not obstruct the Path, thereby contravening the Sangha’s threefold admonition.
The Precept Text has three parts:
first, the person who may commit the offense; second, the method of admonition; third, the establishment of the offense for refusing admonition.
Regarding the second part, the method of admonition, there are two pairs of four phrases:
Regarding the first pair: when a transgression arises, one should first offer private admonition.
Regarding the second pair: if one disregards the private admonition, it is proper that the Saṃgha should offer admonition.
Within the section on the arising of transgressions, the text contains only a single sentence.
As it is said in the Vinaya: Ariṭṭha spoke these words:
"I know what the Buddha has taught; engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path."
Liṭa’s intention was this: "If these things obstruct the Path, why did those in the first two fruits [of the path] engage in sexual desire?
Within the section on private admonition, there are two parts:
the first is an exhortation to cease erroneous speech.
2. From "The World-Honored One is immeasurable" onwards, [the author] refutes that misconception. The refutation states:

when the World-Honored One speaks of "obstructions," he refers to the obstructions to the latter two fruits; however, for the first two fruits, the obstructions have already been severed prior to reaching them. This does not mean that they do not obstruct, but rather that they are no longer severed [once those fruits are attained].
Next, the second [stage] is distinguished: if one violates the principle of private admonition, it is proper that the Saṃgha should admonish them.
"When that bhikṣu admonishes this bhikṣu, he stubbornly maintains his position and does not relinquish it" refers to the violation of private admonition.
"From 'That bhikṣu should be admonished three times' onwards, this concerns the admonition by the Saṃgha.
The text has two parts:
first, instructing the Saṃgha on how to admonish him to relinquish [the offense]; second, praising relinquishment as virtuous."
That is to say, what was previously praised becomes its opposite when contradicted, yet here it is established as being in accord with the wholesome.
Sixty-ninth: The precept on complying with a monk who has been formally charged.
Regarding the phrase "knowing such a person": it means knowing that such a person, Riddha, is one who speaks words of desire that do not constitute an obstruction.

"Those for whom the formal act has not been performed" refers to those whom the Saṃgha previously disciplined and censured, but for whom the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for their release from censure has not yet been performed.
The Saṃgha disciplines these three types of persons through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*:
first, those who do not acknowledge their offense; second, those who do not repent for their offense; and third, those who do not relinquish their evil views.
Now, this intention is distinguished according to the third type of transgression; it follows that according to the first two types of transgression, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Regarding the phrase "such wrong view," it refers to the denial of the path of cultivation.
"Not relinquishing" refers to defying the two admonitions of the *saṃgha* in private.
From "acting in common" onwards, it concerns the commission of an offense through compliance.
The seventieth [offense] is the precept concerning following a suspended *śrāmaṇera*.
When a śrāmaṇera declares that his desire does not constitute an obstacle, he is expelled by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

This case is identical in meaning to the formal act (*dharmakarma*) performed against Ariṣṭa, though the terminology differs; for while the full monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*) previously always shared quarters with him, they now prohibit co-residence due to his heterodox views. Thus, it is called "suspension" (*ukkhepanīya*), which is to say, setting him aside.

A śrāmaṇera was previously not always permitted to sit together [with others], but now, due to his wrong views, he is further not allowed to sit together; therefore, this is called "banishment," which is to expel him.
There are four parts to the text of the precepts:
first, the person who commits the offense.
1. The second [section] reveals how the śrāmaṇera held wrong views and defied admonition. 2.
From "That bhikṣu should say to this śrāmaṇera" onwards, it shows that because of his wrong views, he must be expelled (nāśana).
3. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it concerns the formal act of expulsion (nāśanīya-karman) and the resulting offense.
The text concerning the method of admonition in the second section has three parts:
first, identifying the śrāmaṇera who commits the offense;
second, from the phrase "speaking these words" onwards, identifying the method of admonition.
Third, regarding "not relinquishing," this distinguishes the refusal to heed the Sangha’s admonition.
Within the second method of admonition, there are two pairs of four propositions, which should be understood according to the preceding explanation.

Regarding the third proposition, which distinguishes the *pārivāsika* (banishment) rite: according to the Vinaya, one must perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) and three subsequent proclamations (*karmavācana*) to banish them.
The present precept text is based on the formal ritual (karmavācanā) regarding the verbal expulsion of a monk by the Saṃgha.
Precept Number Seventy-one: The Precept Against Disparaging Others’ Wholesome Exhortations.

When another person encourages one to train according to the Dharma through the Vinaya, to treat them with contempt and evasion, failing to respect this virtuous friend, and to falsely claim to seek something superior while disparaging this good person, one incurs an offense.
Previously, he did not accept admonition and spoke no words, but instead acted in direct defiance by making this current false pretext.
Even before the matter could be contradicted by facts, the Vinaya text states that he has clearly committed an offense.
If one does not falsely claim [to have renounced them] but truly desires to seek excellence, they are permitted as stated in the text.
Seventy-second: To disparage any single precept constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Within the sūtras there are texts concerning the precepts; to disparage them also constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
To disparage either of the other two Piṭakas constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing).
The seventy-third precept concerns not listening attentively;
in Master Nanshan’s *Xingshichao*, it is termed the "precept against preemptive speech out of fear of being accused."
As recorded in the Vinaya origin story, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing they had committed an offense and fearing others would expose it,
first went to others and said:
"I have only just realized it."
Furthermore, some say:
"This is merely a precept for feigning alarm.
Now, if this were the case, it would be subsumed under the minor false speech [precept]; why then would such a separate precept be necessary?
Upon examining various Vinayas and treatises, they all conclude that listening [to the Dharma] without concentration is not permitted.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣā* (Daolun), fascicle nine, states: "In this context, it is specifically concluded that not listening with a concentrated mind constitutes an offense.
